10.1016/j.scs.2026.107237.title: Addressing synergistic climate-urbanization impacts: A coupled PLUS-ML framework for projecting future LCZ and SUHI
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107237.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107237.abstract: Studies have assessed the individual effects of global warming and urbanization on urban thermal stress, yet the synergistic effects of global warming interacting with both urban expansion and intensification in the urbanization process on surface urban heat island (SUHI) have not been clarified. To analyze these synergy effects, we propose an integrated predictive framework that couples an improved PLUS model for Local Climate Zone (LCZ) transitions and a machine learning-based land surface temperature (LST) prediction module incorporating the global warming signal. Applied to the Wuhan Metropolitan Area (WMA), the proposed framework simulated LCZ and LST patterns from 2020 to 2030 under five scenarios. Utilizing the summer mean LST, near-surface air temperature, and LCZ maps from 2005 to 2020 as training data, the prediction model achieved an R² of 0.82 and RMSE of 0.70 °C. The contributions of urbanization and global warming to the increase of LST from 2020 to 2030 in the Natural Growth Scenario (NGS) are found to be 3.93 °C and 1.59 °C, respectively. The scenario analysis on the spatial variations on the SUHI changes via LCZ reveals that the environmental protection scenario (EPS) associated with the lowest SUHI increase, while the urban development scenario (UDS) corresponds to the highest warming with the spatial-average LST rising up to 0.82 °C in urban LCZ. Targeted strategies are then proposed to alleviate thermal risks and enhance climate resilience in the WMA. This study provides a scientific foundation for designing sustainable urban interventions and climate-resilient development policies amid compound environmental challenges.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107323.title: Towards scenario-conditioned urban renewal using a progressive CP-GAN framework under heat–carbon–wind scenarios
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107323.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107323.abstract: High-density cities face escalating challenges from heat stress, carbon emissions, and reduced airflow. However, optimizing three-dimensional morphologies for urban renewal has been constrained by data complexity and computational bottlenecks, preventing real-time application. To address this gap, this study proposed a progressive conditional generative framework (CP-GAN) that integrated Pix2Pix and CycleGAN to synthesize urban forms conditioned on Local Climate Zones (LCZs) and to evaluate their responses to cooling and carbon-reduction objectives under prescribed near-surface wind conditions. The framework integrated multimodal inputs, including land surface temperature, carbon-emission intensity, and wind speed, with outputs capturing building morphology, land cover, and LCZ classification. The results showed that: (1) CP-GAN outperformed the Pix2Pix baseline, achieving an average SSIM of 0.835 and an R² of 0.792, with lower MSE and competitive PSNR; (2) Cooling-oriented optimization drove marked morphological shifts, reducing Floor Area Ratio (FAR) and Building Height (BH) by 37.6% and 25.9% on average, whereas carbon-focused optimization produced only moderate adjustments; (3) Green Ratio (GR) was a key driver of cooling optimization, increasing by 49.1% on average, but contributed little to carbon reduction, where FAR and BH played a dominant role; (4) Three scenario-conditioned pathways were identified: high-density blocks optimized through reductions in FAR and BH, medium-density blocks through enhanced green continuity and ventilation corridors, and inherently low-carbon parcels through incremental local adjustments. This study demonstrated how CP-GAN framework enables adaptive three-dimensional urban renewal by dynamically balancing heat mitigation, carbon reduction, and wind performance, thus providing a robust pathway for advancing climate-responsive design.

10.1016/j.scs.2025.107099.title: Hybrid WRF-ML modeling for characterizing inter- and intra-LCZ microclimate variability: A case study of Shenzhen, China
10.1016/j.scs.2025.107099.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2025.107099.abstract: Understanding microclimatic variations across Local Climate Zones (LCZs) is crucial for optimizing urban morphology to enhance human thermal comfort and promote sustainable urban environments. While numerous studies have examined the spatio-temporal patterns and underlying mechanisms of thermal environments in different LCZ types, temperature variability within identical LCZs remain insufficiently explored. Moreover, research on other microclimate factors—such as relative humidity (RH) and wind speed (WS)—at both inter- and intra-LCZ scales is limited. In this study, a hybrid modeling framework based on the Weather Research and Forecast (WRF) model was proposed to accurately predict near-surface meteorological fields. It was achieved by refining the Urban Canopy Model (UCM) during the preprocessing stage of the WRF model and then integrating ML algorithms during its postprocessing stage. The predictive performance of four WRF-based datasets was evaluated and compared under relatively stable weather conditions across four seasons. The best-performing ML(XGBoost)-enhanced model dataset was applied to identify multivariate microclimate variations both inter- and intra-LCZs. The analysis was conducted in Shenzhen, a coastal hilly city in southern China. The results revealed that: (1) the WRF-ML hybrid models performed significantly better than the Standard and UCM-refined WRF models, with the optimal XGBoost-enhanced model achieving hourly average RMSE values of 0.613 K for AT, 1.131 % for RH, and 0.207 m/s for WS; (2) unique local geographic conditions, such as coastal surroundings and continuous natural landscapes, significantly influence microclimate variations within urban built-up areas; (3) inter-LCZ microclimate differences were generally within 1.5 K for AT, 9 % for RH, and 0.7 m/s for WS, exceeding intra-LCZ differences; and (4) built-up LCZs could be further divided into 2∼4 subcategories with distinct microclimate conditions, some of which showed relatively favorable microclimate environments during the high temperature period.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107531.title: A multi-stage ROM-enhanced CFD-ML framework for efficient 3D urban wind-field prediction
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107531.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107531.abstract: Rapid assessment of urban wind environments is essential for early-stage sustainable and low-carbon urban design, yet conventional CFD becomes computationally prohibitive when multiple inflow directions and velocities are required. This study proposes a multi-stage ROM-enhanced CFD–ML framework for efficient and physically consistent urban wind-field prediction. A baseline CFD database is constructed using steady RANS simulations with sufficient surrounding-building layers. A reduced-order modeling (ROM) strategy coupled with machine learning reconstructs high-fidelity wind fields at unsampled velocities using a subset of inflow velocities, achieving R² ≥ 0.99 and reducing required CFD cases by at least 40% (e.g., 6 instead of 10 per direction); for two validation urban configurations, this yields savings of approximately 112 h of CFD computation time. Using the ROM-enhanced database, a morphology-driven surrogate is trained with eight urban morphological parameters plus inflow conditions to predict u, v, and w. The best MLP and XGBoost models reach R² > 0.99 for u and v and R² > 0.98 for w, while XGBoost trains markedly faster and is selected. Without additional CFD-based learning on unseen cases, the model delivers high-accuracy 3D wind-field predictions under oblique inflow and different urban layouts, achieving normalized percentage errors below 5% at pedestrian height, while quantitative profile-based metrics confirm preservation of height-dependent flow structures from pedestrian level to rooftop. Compared with conventional CFD, the trained ML model achieves approximately two orders of magnitude computational speedup. SHAP-based interpretability analysis confirms physically meaningful morphology-wind relationships. Overall, the framework offers an efficient, scalable, and interpretable solution for rapid 3D urban wind assessment in early-stage design and urban climate studies.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.108067.title: Quantifying the nonlinear interactions between low-carbon development and urban resilience for urban renewal: An LV–ML–Vivid analysis
10.1016/j.scs.2026.108067.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.108067.abstract: Low-carbon development (LcD) and resilience-building (RB) are increasingly viewed as an integrated whole in urban policy. Urban renewal serves as a key component of urban development policy and provides a concrete practical setting for coordinating the low-carbon transition with the enhancement of resilience. This research constructed LcD and RB indices using social, economic, environmental, energy, infrastructure, technological, and policy data from 2011 to 2023 for 13 cities in Jiangsu Province, China, and classified the interactive states between both at the city level using the Lotka–Volterra model. Subsequently, candidate indicators and coordination metrics were examined for predictive associations using machine learning regression models and the Vivid framework. Results showed that: (1) Relationships between cities and across periods exhibit varying patterns of LcD–RB. Single-benefit were more common than mutualistic or sub-mutualistic states, although some cities develop more mutually beneficial relationships during particular periods; (2) PCRS exhibited the highest model-based variable importance, while ECP, TSP, MOP, and ECR also showed relatively high predictive contributions; (3) Vivid analysis identified comparatively strong non-additive predictive interactions for the PCRS–ECP, PCRS–EST, and MOP–TP combinations. Research findings advance understanding of the relationship between low-carbon and resilient development in urban renewal, contributing empirical evidence for integrating low-carbon and resilience objectives within urban renewal policies.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107978.title: Reconstruction of fine-scale turbulence using GAN- and diffusion-based super-resolution models for Urban Air Mobility applications
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107978.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107978.abstract: This study evaluated deep-learning-based super-resolution (SR) models at an extreme 20× scaling factor using the Parallelized Large-Eddy Simulation Model (PALM) over a real urban environment. Such an evaluation addresses the practical need for fine-scale turbulent flows in complex urban environments relevant to Urban Air Mobility (UAM) applications. To investigate SR strategies, we employed two models: the Enhanced Super-Resolution Generative Adversarial Network (ESRGAN), which directly performs 20× scaling, and a pretrained Latent Diffusion Model (LDM), trained on natural images, which uses a fixed 4× network with interpolation to achieve an overall resolution increase from 100 m to 5 m. The experiments provide a comparative assessment of GAN- and diffusion-based models for reconstructing fine-scale wind components (u, v, and w). The analysis evaluates not only visual reconstruction quality but also the physical consistency of the reconstructed fields, including the preservation of flow structures and energy spectra. ESRGAN effectively reconstructed fine-scale turbulent structures with good agreement in statistical metrics, whereas the pretrained LDM produced smoother reconstructions that preserved large-scale flow features. One-dimensional power spectral density analysis revealed that both models aligned well with the HR reference in the intermediate-to-high wavenumber range. However, at the highest wavenumbers, ESRGAN exhibited irregular spectral fluctuations, while the LDM showed a more rapid energy decay. Notably, both models demonstrated closer agreement with HR under stronger turbulence conditions. The proposed framework enables near real-time 3D turbulent field reconstruction, highlighting its potential for practical UAM applications.

10.1016/j.scs.2025.107087.title: Integrated remote sensing and machine learning approach for LST trend analysis and SUHI detection in the semi-arid climate of Kabul province using Google Earth Engine
10.1016/j.scs.2025.107087.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2025.107087.abstract: This study investigates the spatiotemporal dynamics of Land Surface Temperature (LST) and Surface Urban Heat Island (SUHI) intensity in Kabul Province, Afghanistan (2000–2024), by integrating multi-source satellite data with climatic, topographic, and surface biophysical variables to identify environmental drivers and predict spatial patterns. Monthly LST time series were standardized and analyzed using the Mann–Kendall test and Sen’s slope estimator, while the Random Forest (RF) model was applied to classify and predict LST across Land Use and Land Cover (LULC) classes. LST peaked at 47 °C in July 2023 and dropped to –4 °C in January 2006. Daytime mean LSTs were highest in bare land (41 °C) and urban areas (38 °C), followed by water (34 °C) and vegetation (32 °C). At night, urban surfaces remained the warmest (23 °C). The Mann–Kendall test revealed a nonsignificant long-term trend (p = 0.145, Z = –1.459), indicating short-term seasonal fluctuations. Hotspot analysis identified significant summer SUHI clustering in highly urbanized and sparsely vegetated areas (Kabul City, Deh Sabz, Bagrami, Surobi), while winter SUHI was minimal due to snow cover and higher surface albedo. The RF model achieved strong performance (RMSE = 2.33–2.46; r = 0.61–0.88) across MODIS, Landsat, and ERA5 datasets. This integrated remote sensing and machine learning framework provides a scalable approach for monitoring urban thermal environments and supports climate-adaptive urban planning and sustainable land management in semi-arid regions.
keywords: Daytime and nighttime land surface temperature

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107141.title: Reconstruction of Pedestrian-Level pollutant distributions in urban street canyon using physics-informed neural network
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107141.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107141.abstract: Rapid urban expansion, coupled with an increasing number of motor vehicles, has rendered street canyons critical zones for PM2.5 accumulation. However, the limited density of on-site monitoring and the considerable computational cost of conventional computational fluid dynamics simulations impede accurate and real-time assessment of pollution exposure at the pedestrian level. This study proposes a framework termed PINN-RAS, which integrates a physics-informed neural network (PINN) with a residual-softmax adaptive sampling (RAS) strategy. This framework enables the reconstruction of fine-scale pollution distributions based on sparse observational data. First, the incorporation of physical constraints enables the PINN model to maintain predictive robustness as the proportion of training data decreases progressively from 80% to 5%. It captures dominant vortices and pollutant gradients within the canyon, with overall R2 values consistently exceeding 0.8. Second, under simulated measurement noise, the model demonstrates strong local error convergence. Prediction errors remain confined to narrow boundary regions, achieving an R2 of 0.81, which outperforms baseline models including convolutional neural and long short-term memory networks. Third, the RAS strategy dynamically allocates sampling points in regions with high residuals and sharp concentration gradients, thereby enhancing coverage of critical zones. The reconstruction model achieves an R2 of 0.85, while the mean squared error and mean absolute error are reduced to 0.11 and 0.16, respectively, thereby enabling finer-scale reconstruction using an equivalent data proportion. This method provides a cost-effective and efficient solution for real-time, high-resolution air quality assessment and facilitates precise health risk assessment and control at the pedestrian level.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107228.title: Advancing climate justice for vulnerable groups: Optimizing spatial configuration of urban blue–green infrastructure to mitigate heat risks leveraging explainable machine learning
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107228.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107228.abstract: Climate change and urbanization are driving an increase in heat risks, subjecting vulnerable groups to more severe climate injustice. However, recognition and response strategies to the compound heat risks faced by these groups remain limited. As a critical climate adaptation measure and a key component of nature-based solution (NbS), urban blue–green infrastructure (UBGI) holds substantial potential for mitigating such risks. Therefore, we conducted a case study of Hangzhou’s main urban area to assess the compound heat risks of vulnerable groups across the dimensions of hazard, exposure, and vulnerability, and to further examine how the spatial configuration of UBGI moderated these risks. The results reveal clear spatial heterogeneity in heat risks among vulnerable groups. High-heat-risk areas for low-income individuals clustered in the southwest of the study area, especially Shuangpu; migrant workers and older adults faced high risks in old urban-core neighborhoods (e.g., Changqing, Chaoming, Xiaoying); and children showed a dual pattern, with high-risk areas in both the southwestern periphery and the historic city center. In terms of proportions, low-income individuals accounted for the largest share of high-risk areas (16.61 %), followed by migrant workers (15.20 %), children (12.09 %), and older adults (8.72 %). Across all vulnerable groups, blue infrastructure accessibility and connectivity, as well as green infrastructure accessibility and area, showed significant negative associations with heat risks. Among various vulnerable groups, the most influential indicators varied: blue infrastructure connectivity for children, blue infrastructure accessibility for older adults, green infrastructure area for migrant workers, and green infrastructure aggregation for low-income individuals, which exhibited different response thresholds. Drawing on these findings, we proposed implementing targeted interventions through both uniform and tailored UBGI spatial configuration strategies to mitigate heat risks among vulnerable groups. This study offers a robust scientific foundation for differentiated adaptation strategies and equity-oriented urban planning, thereby advancing climate justice.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107278.title: A systematic review on the integrations of CFD and artificial intelligence for the future perspectives of built environment: Multi-scale approaches from room to city
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107278.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107278.abstract:
ABSTRACT
The integration of Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) and Artificial Intelligence (AI) have offered a transformative solution to CFD's prohibitive computational cost in built environment application. While AI surrogates successfully accelerate simulations, a systematic review of 229 studies revealed a fundamental disconnect: studies are overwhelmingly distributed across a single spatial scale, such as a room, a building, or a city. True multi-scale integration, essential for capturing the interconnected physics of the built environment, remains critically under-explored. This core challenge is compounded by persistent hurdles in model generalization, physical consistency, and research reproducibility. This review synthesizes these limitations to propose a comprehensive framework that pivots from isolated models toward a unified, physically consistent approach. We advocate for developing hierarchical, physics-informed learning strategies built upon sophisticated benchmark datasets to ensure reliable and scalable information transfer across room-, building-, and city-scales. This work provides the necessary roadmap to bridge this critical gap, enabling robust, multi-scale simulation for sustainable design and operation.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107202.title: Spatiotemporal dynamics and multidimensional drivers of urban diurnal temperature range: Evidence from integrated learning at the national scale in China
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107202.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107202.abstract: Urbanization and global warming are profoundly altering the diurnal temperature range (DTR), a key indicator of climate change with direct implications for public health and urban resilience. Yet, systematic evidence disentangling DTR dynamics across climatic zones at the national scale remains scarce. Using 1 km resolution MODIS LST data for China (2010–2020), this study integrates spatiotemporal trend analysis with explainable machine learning to characterize national DTR patterns and identify their heterogeneous drivers. The results show that: (1) daytime surface warming (+0.013 °C yr⁻¹) has outpaced nighttime warming (+0.008 °C yr⁻¹), leading to an overall slight increase in DTR, with the trend most pronounced in the warm temperate zone; (2) natural systems exert the strongest influence (42.1 %), with proximity to water bodies acting as the most critical regulator—reducing DTR by 2–3 °C within 5 km—while vegetation effects are strongly climate-dependent; (3) urban physical morphology exerts dual impacts, as high built-up density generally amplifies DTR, whereas taller buildings mitigate it by enhancing ventilation; and (4) socioeconomic factors overall moderate DTR, with population density showing the most consistent effect, while nighttime light intensity anomalously amplifies DTR in humid regions. By systematically revealing the climatic heterogeneity of DTR drivers, this study underscores the pivotal role of water bodies and urban form in regulating urban heat. The findings provide a scientific basis for context-specific nature-based solutions and resilience-oriented planning strategies to mitigate thermal risks under accelerating climate change and urbanization.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107307.title: Nonlinear drivers of canopy and surface urban heat islands across China’s climate zones: marginal and interaction effects from explainable machine learning
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107307.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107307.abstract: As urbanization accelerates, the urban heat island effect has emerged as a key challenge for urban environments and sustainability. However, systematic cross climate-zone comparisons of the nonlinear drivers of the canopy urban heat island (CUHI) and the surface urban heat island (SUHI) remain limited. Here, across 300 cities spanning the major climate zones of China, we integrate multi-source datasets including meteorological observations, land surface temperature, and reanalysis products. We compile factors describing meteorology, surface biophysics, socio-economic, landscape pattern metrics, and urban morphology, and apply an interpretable machine-learning framework to comparatively assess the spatiotemporal patterns, drivers, marginal effects, and interaction mechanisms of CUHI and SUHI. We find that: (1) CUHI intensity (CUHII) in most cities is concentrated within 0–1 °C, whereas SUHI intensity (SUHII) is stronger and more variable. In warm-temperate cities, the mean daytime summer SUHII approaches 5 °C, and the diurnal and seasonal contrasts of SUHII are markedly larger than those of CUHII. (2) CUHII is mainly governed by meteorological and surface biophysical factors, with the influence of socio-economic variables strengthening at night and in winter. By contrast, SUHII is dominated by surface properties across scenarios and is more sensitive to urban morphology. (3) Multiple factors exhibit thresholds and “warming/cooling plateaus”, and SUHII is more sensitive to interaction effects than CUHII. Within the same climate zone, the dominant combinations of urban heat island (UHI) drivers show overall commonalities, yet their relative contributions vary with local conditions such as city size and development intensity. Our findings provide key quantitative evidence to support climate-zone-specific, fine-grained urban heat mitigation and climate adaptation strategies.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107287.title: Remote sensing-based PM2.5 inversion and explainable AI analysis of urban environmental drivers in Harbin
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107287.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107287.abstract: Fine particulate matter (PM2.5) poses a serious threat to public health, contributing to respiratory and cardiovascular diseases and premature mortality worldwide. Urban morphology (UM), landscape pattern (LP), and socio-economic (SE) factors play critical roles in regulating pollutant accumulation and dispersion, particularly in cold-climate cities where winter heating emissions, limited atmospheric mixing, and unfavorable topographic conditions often exacerbate pollution levels. However, the nonlinear effects and interaction mechanisms among these driving factors remain insufficiently understood. To address this gap, this study proposes a two-stage analytical framework integrating physically constrained deep learning and explainable machine learning. First, multi-source remote sensing data and physical constraints were incorporated into a deep learning model to generate high-resolution PM2.5 inversion results. Second, an interpretable machine learning approach (XGBoost–SHAP) was employed to quantify the effects of UM, LP, and SE variables on PM2.5 concentrations in Harbin, China. The results show that tree cover ratio (PER_Tree), Normalized Difference Built-up Index (NDBI), mean building height (BH_Mean), and population density (POP) are the most influential spatial indicators across seasons. PER_Tree and Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) exhibit strong negative effects on PM2.5, with threshold values around 65–70 % and 0.3, respectively, whereas NDBI (> –0.2) and BH_Mean (> 10 m) are positively associated with pollution levels, particularly during winter. SHAP interaction analysis further reveals that green infrastructure mitigates pollution effectively only under favorable morphological conditions. Overall, this study advances the integration of remote sensing and interpretable machine learning for urban environmental modeling and provides actionable insights for sustainable urban planning and environmental governance in cold-climate, industrialized cities characterized by centralized heating systems, strong seasonal emission patterns, and topographic constraints.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107376.title: Developing an urban heat vulnerability index based on local climate zones: A hybrid entropy–random forest GIS framework
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107376.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107376.abstract: Rapid urbanization and climate change are intensifying heat stress in cities, yet assessments often overlook the physical diversity of urban form across different climatic contexts. This study develops an Urban Heat Vulnerability (UHV) index, with application to a semi-arid city (Irbid, Jordan), while maintaining transferability across different climate zones. The objectives are to: (i) assess exposure, sensitivity, and adaptive capacity across Local Climate Zones (LCZs), (ii) compare indicator weighting using the Entropy Weight Method and Random Forest Regression (RFR), and (iii) identify vulnerable LCZ classes, and quantify the influence of LCZs parameters on heat vulnerability. A GIS-based LCZ map at 250 × 250 m resolution was created using urban canopy parameters and integrated with thermal, demographic, morphological, and accessibility indicators to build three component indices. Indicator weights were derived using Entropy and RFR, and the weights were combined within a regularized multiplicative model to compute the UHV index. ANOVA was applied to evaluate differences among LCZs classes and agreement between weighting methods. Results show that exposure is highest in compact and bare LCZs. At the same time, sensitivity and adaptive capacity are strongly influenced by urban morphology, with LCZ type explaining a substantial proportion of their variation. Overall, UHV is greatest in compact mid- and low-rise LCZs and lowest in vegetated classes. Geographically Weighted Regression (GWR) further reveals spatial non-stationarity in these relationships, providing localized insights for targeted mitigation. The proposed LCZ-based hybrid weighting framework provides a transferable and scalable tool for urban heat risk assessment, supporting climate-adaptive planning across diverse urban environments.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107469.title: Wildland-urban interface delineation using self-adaptive thresholding informed by historical wildfire patterns: a case study using very-high-resolution satellite imagery and deep learning algorithm
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107469.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107469.abstract: The rapid urbanization and ecological restoration initiatives have generated extensive wildland-urban interface (WUI) zones in China, where escalating wildfire risks now critically threaten both community safety and ecological integrity. The challenges in transferability of delineation criteria and precise acquisition of mapping elements hinder effective WUI fire management. We proposed a very-high-resolution satellite-driven WUI delineation framework for Shenyang City, utilizing a transfer learning-enhanced UNet algorithm that significantly improved building footprint extraction accuracy (93.5 %). An optimization objective function, informed by historical wildfire patterns and gradient boosting regression, enabled self-adaptive threshold derivation for effective intermix and interface WUI delineation. Cross validation against two well-established WUI products demonstrated well performance of our approach in local scale, achieving a 51 % overlap with actual fire-affected areas, which surpassed benchmark datasets (18.7 % and 12.2 %). This spatially explicit framework enhances localized fire resilience planning for WUI areas by enabling the integration of local wildfire characteristics and landscape attributes. These efforts are critical for addressing knowledge gaps in regions where explicit WUI delineation guidelines are currently absent

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107640.title: Designing sponge cities in data-scarce contexts: a machine learning–enabled land cover dynamics and urban hydrologic response framework for nature-based flood resilience
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107640.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107640.abstract: Urban land use and land cover (LULC) change profoundly alters natural surfaces, accelerates runoff, and increases flood risks. However, the coupling between land cover dynamics and urban hydrologic responses (LCDUHR), and its implications for nature-based mitigation, remains poorly understood in data-scarce regions. This study bridges this gap by integrating multi-temporal remote sensing, machine learning (ML), and hydrologic–hydraulic simulation (SWMM 5.2) to assess land-cover-driven hydrologic responses and evaluate sustainable flood mitigation options in Shahjalal Uposhahar, Sylhet, Bangladesh. Ten ML-based models analyzed satellite imagery (2003–2023) and projected LULC to 2033, outperforming conventional classification approaches. Results show that 26.70% of natural surfaces were converted to built-up areas between 2003 and 2023, increasing surface runoff by 11.89–26.97 mm across 2–100-year return periods. By 2033, imperviousness is projected to increase by an additional 2% (relative to 2023), accompanied by continued declines in water bodies and barren land, further exacerbating pluvial flooding. Twelve nature-based solutions (NbS) were modeled as sponge landscape interventions to assess flood mitigation potential. Bioretention ponds achieved the greatest reductions, with a 75% reduction in peak runoff, 27.11–30.15% in runoff volume, and 34.08–50.61% in total flooding, while rain gardens, infiltration trenches, and green roofs also performed effectively. Despite these improvements, existing drainage capacity remains insufficient under extreme storms. This study provides data-driven, spatially explicit insights for designing NbS-integrated urban drainage systems, supporting Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) 6, 11, 13, and 15, and advancing the development of resilient, flood-adaptive cities in rapidly urbanizing, data-limited environments.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107561.title: Physics-informed sensor placement for street canyon wind field reconstruction
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107561.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107561.abstract: Urban wind field reconstruction plays a critical role in pedestrian wind comfort assessment, pollutant dispersion analysis, and urban wind environmental management. However, experimental and field measurements are inherently sparse due to the high cost and limited deployability of sensors, making accurate reconstruction of high-resolution wind fields challenging. Existing optimal sensor placement (OSP) strategies are predominantly data-driven and often neglect the governing physical laws of fluid flow, which can result in physically suboptimal sensor configurations. This study proposes a physics-informed sensor placement framework that tightly couples optimal sensor selection with wind field reconstruction using Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs). Specifically, a greedy active learning strategy is developed, where sensor locations are iteratively selected based on CFD-based reconstruction errors and the geometric importance of latent features learned by the PINN, while enforcing spatial separation constraints to ensure practical deployability. The proposed framework is evaluated using high-fidelity Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes simulations of a two-dimensional street canyon. Results demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves high reconstruction accuracy for both streamwise and vertical velocity components with a limited number of sensors. Compared with random sampling, QR pivoting, and conventional wind tunnel sensor configurations, the framework produces superior reconstruction accuracy. The proposed framework offers a scalable pathway toward physics-consistent sensor deployment in urban environments and has potential for applications in urban wind environmental assessment.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107747.title: Wind amplification induced by high-rise buildings and identification of local wind-prone neighborhoods using a CFD-machine learning framework
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107747.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107747.abstract: High-rise buildings embedded within residential neighborhoods can substantially modify pedestrian-level wind environments, while coupled effects of central high-rise structures and their surrounding built forms remain insufficiently quantified. This study develops an integrated framework that combines Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) simulations with machine learning (ML) techniques to rapidly map city-scale potential wind acceleration hotspots. A comprehensive parametric analysis of the wind speed ratio K is conducted using CFD based on eight central building heights (Hc = b, 2b, 3b, 4b, 5b, 6b, 8b and 10b, where b is the building width), three surrounding building heights (hs = b, 2b and 3b) and four building densities (λp = 0.44, 0.25, 0.16 and 0.11). Results reveal that wind amplification is governed by combined morphological effects rather than a simple monotonic relationship with building height and density. When surrounding buildings are low (hs= b), accelerated wind zones appear near front corners of the higher central building, where K increases with greater central building height and lower building density. In contrast, when Hc < hs, the maximum wind speed ratio Kmax generally decreases with declining density, ranging from 1.01 ∼ 1.43 at λp = 0.44 to 0.71∼1.05 at λp = 0.11. When Hc/hs = 10, the total area ratio of the high wind speed ratio region ARhigh across all building densities reaches its largest value of about 217.50%. SHAP-enhanced ML models identify the height ratio (Hc/hs) as the dominant predictor of Kmax, with larger ratios consistently producing stronger winds. By combining morphological parameters with the ML model, spatial maps of Kmax are generated for densely built cities in China- Guangzhou and Shenzhen, revealing that dense central and western areas are more susceptible to wind acceleration. These results provide new insights into wind behavior around high-rise buildings and support an efficient data-driven framework for screening wind amplification zones.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107699.title: A holistic approach to seismic risk by integrating preparedness into hybrid deep learning and ANP-based spatial modeling: A case study of Coimbatore city, India
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107699.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107699.abstract: Densely populated urban centers like Coimbatore city, India, with overlooked seismic events, require robust seismic risk assessments that extend beyond standard models. This study develops an integrated framework to evaluate hazard, vulnerability, and site- effect amplification potential across 24 indicators, explicitly incorporating preparedness as a moderating factor in vulnerability. A Convolutional Neural Network-Extreme Gradient Boosting (CNN–XGB) hybrid model was used to map eleven physical indicators for site-effect amplification, demonstrating strong performance (precision, recall, and F-1 score of 0.82) by combining deep learning spatial recognition with ensemble predictive accuracy. The hazard map was prepared using the Deterministic Seismic Hazard Assessment (DSHA) method. An integrated vulnerability map was developed using the Analytic Network Process (ANP), to synthesize ten interdependent physical and social vulnerability indicators, including household density, building intensity, demographics, socio-economics, and emergency service accessibility. Preparedness was mapped using ward-level data from the 27-item Individual Earthquake Readiness Index (IERI) and the 20-item Community Earthquake Readiness Index (CERI), based on survey responses. Spatial data from government records, Sentinel and SRTM (30-meter resolution) were rasterized, classified by the Jenks method, and integrated into a high-resolution seismic risk map. Results reveal critical hotspots in the central and southwestern wards, where high hazard and vulnerability coincide with low-to-moderate preparedness. Findings emphasize the need for preparedness-inclusive models enabling proactive, location-specific policy interventions, such as extending workplace readiness to households, shared emergency-box systems, equitable leadership promotion, and retrofitting. This adaptable framework supports anticipatory disaster risk reduction strategies in rapidly urbanizing regions by strengthening social resilience.
keywords: Convolutional neural network-extreme gradient boosting (CNN-XGB) model

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107890.title: An iterative graph neural operator with propagation field for urban-scale wind field reconstruction
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107890.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107890.abstract: Accurately predicting climate and environmental variables is essential in a wide range of engineering applications, and Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) has been widely used as a key analytical tool in these fields. However, conventional CFD simulations have limitations due to high computational costs and sensitivity to boundary conditions, restricting their use in large-scale or real-time scenarios. While data-driven CFD surrogate models have emerged as promising alternatives, they still face challenges in terms of handling unstructured meshes and accommodating flexible sensor configurations. To address these limitations, this study proposes an iterative graph neural operator with a Propagated confidence Field for steady-state CFD surrogate modeling on unstructured meshes. Instead of predicting the flow field all at once, this model iteratively improves the solution by reflecting the convergence behavior of steady-state CFD. A Propagated confidence Field was introduced to represent the spatial range of information obtained from inlet and sensor nodes. Validation results show that the proposed model maintains stable reconstruction performance across sparse and flexible sensor configurations within the tested urban CFD system. Error metrics decrease as sensor density increases, while cosine similarity improves, indicating enhanced reconstruction accuracy. However, once sensor density exceeds a certain level, the effect of performance improvement decreases. This model maintains the flow direction and overall structure even when observational data is insufficient. The proposed framework provides a discretization-invariant approach capable of flexibly handling varying sensor configurations. Future work will focus on improving physical consistency through physics-informed extensions.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107939.title: A SHAP-enhanced physics-informed neural network for interpretable and high accuracy prediction of neighborhood thermal environments
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107939.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107939.abstract: Accurate and rapid prediction of neighborhood scale air temperature is critical for heat risk identification, climate adaptive urban design, and thermal comfort assessment. However, existing thermal environment prediction methods are largely dominated by computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations and data-driven models, and are constrained either by high computational costs or by limited consideration of heat transfer physics. This study aims to develop a SHAP-enhanced physics-informed neural network (S-PINN) for neighborhood scale air temperature prediction by integrating data-driven learning with governing heat transfer equations. First, neighborhood thermal environment data were obtained from field measurements and numerical simulations. Second, a PINN prediction model was developed by embedding the heat transfer equations of the neighborhood thermal environment and training it with simulated air temperature outputs under physical constraints. Third, SHAP was used to quantify the contributions of key influencing factors, and the resulting attribution information was incorporated to refine the PINN model, thereby proposing the S-PINN. Results indicate that sky view factor (SVF) and green coverage ratio (GCR) are the dominant morphological drivers of air temperature, with structural equation model (SEM) path coefficients of 0.643 and −0.428, respectively. S-PINN consistently outperformed multiple linear regression (MLR), multilayer perceptron (MLP), convolutional neural network (CNN), and baseline PINN. Relative to MLR, S-PINN reduced mean relative error (MRE) by 42.00%–50.93% and achieved absolute increases R2 by 0.108–0.447. Relative to MLP and CNN, MRE decreased by 12.79%–35.81%, and R2 increased by 1.71%–14.87%. Compared to PINN, MRE was reduced by 3.10%–7.11%, and R2 increased by 0.63%–2.38%. This study incorporates SHAP explanations as structural priors into the PINN training, improving prediction accuracy, physical consistency, and interpretability simultaneously. The proposed framework provides an actionable pathway for neighborhood scale heat risk identification and the morphologically optimized thermal environment control strategies.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107961.title: Long-term probabilistic urban wind assessment for resilient urban air mobility using physics-informed surrogate modeling
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107961.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107961.abstract: Urban air mobility (UAM) is being considered as a future component of sustainable urban transportation, but its operation is strongly affected by the complex wind environment in dense cities. Reliable long-term characterization of building-resolved urban wind conditions remains difficult, as high-fidelity large-eddy simulations (LES) are computationally too expensive for continuous application under realistic meteorological conditions. This study develops a physics-informed surrogate modeling framework to reconstruct urban wind fields by combining LES data with minute-resolution meteorological observations. The framework enables efficient reconstruction of building-scale wind conditions over extended time periods and is applied to a high-rise district in Yeouido, Seoul, using one year of observational data. The results show strong spatial and temporal variability of urban wind conditions, governed by building configuration and wind direction. Conventional mean-based metrics are found to underestimate short-term wind fluctuations within the urban canopy. Probabilistic analysis across representative urban morphologies within the Yeouido district indicates that operational usability remains below 34% of the year in the unperturbed baseline assessment. When instrument-level measurement and surrogate residual uncertainties are propagated through the assessment, operational usability remains well below the commonly recommended 95% operational target. These results demonstrate the capability of the proposed framework for long-term, time-resolved analysis of urban wind environments. The approach provides a computationally efficient basis for probabilistic wind assessment and supports risk-informed planning of urban air mobility systems.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107934.title: Physics-informed optimization of urban greening for pollen-induced allergenic risk mitigation: A scalable framework powered by built environment-embedded dispersion modeling and parallel computing
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107934.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107934.abstract: The expansion of urban green infrastructure is a cornerstone of sustainable city development. However, the associated rise in pollen-induced allergies poses a significant public health challenge. Current allergenic risk assessment methods fail to account for the complex interactions between airborne pollen, inhomogeneous wind fields, and the built environment. To bridge this gap, this study proposes an urban greening optimization framework based on a built environment-embedded Gaussian Plume Model. The method integrates tree-involved computational fluid dynamics simulations, building occlusion effects, and wind spectra analysis to quantify allergenic risks at a high resolution. A case study of a 4.2 km2 urban area containing over 18,000 trees demonstrates the framework's efficacy. Results reveal that the original greening scheme generates a cumulative high-risk area of 8.0%, with specific wind directions exacerbating risks to over 10%. Through iterative design with the proposed method, a low-cost canopy contraction scheme reduces the high-risk area to 4.9%, while an ecological reconstruction scheme achieves a reduction to 3.3%. Furthermore, a process-based parallel computing technique is developed to accelerate the computationally intensive assessment, thus making iterative design optimization a tangible reality for urban planners. This study addresses the critical conflict between urban greening expansion and the rising prevalence of pollinosis, providing decision-makers with a scientific, quantitative tool to balance ecological benefits with public health in sustainable urban design.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.108069.title: Urban flood risk prediction based on the hybrid sampling of imbalanced data and deep learning model
10.1016/j.scs.2026.108069.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.108069.abstract: Existing urban flood risk prediction models often suffer from data imbalance in risk samples, which significantly degrades their predictive performance, especially in identifying high risk events. This study proposes an urban flood risk prediction model based on hybrid sampling and deep learning to address this issue. Specifically, Wasserstein Generative Adversarial Network (W-GAN) was employed to oversample the minority-class very high and high risk samples, while Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise (DBSCAN) combined was used to undersample the majority-class low and very low risk samples. Based on the dataset obtained after hybrid sampling, a convolutional neural network (CNN)-based urban flood risk prediction model was developed, and the effects of different sampling strategies on prediction performance were systematically investigated. Taking Haidian Island, Hainan Province, China as the study area, the number of very low risk samples was about ten times that of very high risk samples, indicating a class imbalance in the dataset. After hybrid sampling optimization, the macro-averaged F1-score of the CNN model increased from 0.8448 to 0.8949 compared with the model trained on the imbalanced dataset. In particular, the F1-score for the very high risk level increased from 0.7654 to 0.9474. Among different sampling strategies, the hybrid sampling strategy outperformed single oversampling and single undersampling, while the sample size also affected the prediction performance. This study can provide scientific support for the precise prevention and control of urban flood risks.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.108047.title: Beyond the CFD/AI neutral sectorial kernel: A comprehensive post-processing framework for hourly NO2 assessment integrating atmospheric stability, temporal inertia and chemical conversion
10.1016/j.scs.2026.108047.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.108047.abstract: Micro-scale urban air quality models, particularly Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) and Artificial Intelligence (AI) architectures, face significant computational issues when predicting high-frequency pollutant concentrations. To maintain computational feasibility, such models conventionally rely on steady-state and neutral atmospheric assumptions, which allow for a sectorial approach, avoiding direct CFD computation of every hour-by-hour simulations. However, it fails to capture highly transient meteorological and photochemical dynamics. To address this limitation, this study introduces a comprehensive post-processing framework designed to dynamically reconstruct hourly NO2 concentrations from isothermal (neutral stability) steady-state simulations. Applied to a dual-resolution observational dataset collected in Antwerp, Belgium (hourly data at traffic-oriented air quality monitoring stations (AQMS) and monthly passive samplers), the methodology integrates targeted corrections for sub-grid meandering, boundary-layer ventilation, inertial carry-over, and photochemistry. The evaluation at the AQMS shows a strong reduction of temporal variance and bias for both models. Importantly, a novel background-relative correlation criterion (CR) shows that the framework restores an hourly temporal correlation equal to that of the regional background alone, which the neutral models degrade, while simultaneously enabling accurate estimation of local concentration magnitudes and biases. While restructuring hourly dynamics at the AQMS, the framework leaves the spatial correlations at the monthly passive samplers unchanged. Finally, a Shapley-based attribution analysis highlights the framework’s paradigm-specific adaptability, showing that the meandering module contributes most for the CFD model and the ventilation module for the AI model. This framework offers a computationally viable methodology to improve hourly urban air quality predictions from neutral sectorial simulations, with transferability to other cities and climates remaining to be assessed.

10.1016/j.scs.2025.107039.title: A novel cross-city video-based ensemble deep learning model for air quality estimation
10.1016/j.scs.2025.107039.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2025.107039.abstract: Air pollution poses a significant threat to sustainable urban development, public health, and environmental quality in cities worldwide. Accurate PM2.5 estimation is essential for effective urban planning and pollution control. However, existing methods often rely on single static images, which fail to capture the dynamic temporal nature of pollution and typically require city-specific training, thereby limiting their transferability to new cities. To address these issues, this study proposes the Cross-City Air Quality Estimation Network (CCAQE-Net), a novel video-based hybrid deep learning model designed to estimate PM2.5 concentrations in unseen cities. The model employs the Video Vision Transformer (ViViT) with self-attention mechanism to extract spatiotemporal pollution features from videos, and then applies a Random Forest Regressor (RFR) to map complex non-linear relationships and estimate PM2.5. We evaluated the model using the PCCAQV dataset, which contains 8640 hourly outdoor air quality videos from six major Pakistani cities: Karachi, Multan, Faisalabad, Lahore, Rawalpindi, and Islamabad. The inclusion of data from multiple cities enables the model to learn comprehensive spatiotemporal air pollution dynamics under varying meteorological conditions, atmospheric interactions, pollution sources, and topographical features, thus enhancing its robustness and generalizability. To rigorously assess the model’s ability, we adopted a Leave-One-City-Out (LOCO) approach: training on five cities and testing on the sixth, iteratively repeating this process for all six cities. The experimental results demonstrate that the proposed model achieves superior performance, with an average R2 of 0.97, RMSE of 1.42 μg/m3, MAE of 1.14 μg/m3, and MAPE of 10.87 %, outperforming current state-of-the-art models across all evaluated cities.

10.1016/j.scs.2025.107058.title: Impacts of block morphological evolution on thermal environment during urbanization: Application of random forest and SHAP method
10.1016/j.scs.2025.107058.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2025.107058.abstract: During urbanization, changes in block morphology substantially influence the urban thermal environment. Understanding the nonlinear and interactive effects between block morphology and thermal conditions is essential for effective thermal regulation. However, most existing studies rely on linear assumptions and single thermal indicators, limiting their ability to capture these complex relationships. This study takes the Xiangxue area of Guangzhou as a case study. An ENVI-met model was developed using multi-source data to simulate the impacts of morphological evolution on the summer thermal environment from 2007 to 2023. Four indicators, including air temperature, relative humidity (RH), wind velocity ratio (WVR), and physiological equivalent temperature (PET), were employed to comprehensively characterize the thermal environment. A random forest (RF) regression model, combined with SHAP interpretation and partial dependence plot (PDP) visualization, was applied to elucidate the nonlinear relationships between morphology parameters and thermal indicators, as well as the interactive effects among these parameters. The results show that with urbanization, impervious surface coverage (ISC), sky view factor (SVF), building density (BD), and average building height (ABH) increased continuously, while vegetation cover (VC) declined. These changes led to higher temperatures, lower humidity, weaker wind, and markedly deteriorated thermal comfort. Among these factors, ISC, SVF, and VC emerged as the primary determinants of thermal conditions, displaying significant nonlinear response patterns exhibiting distinct nonlinear response patterns, as well as evident threshold and interaction effects. The findings suggest that maintaining the ISC below 30 %, keeping the SVF around 0.4, and increasing the VC to approximately 40 % can effectively improve the local thermal environment. Furthermore, improving ventilation in high-density areas and optimizing the use of vertical space can enhance thermal regulation capacity. This study provides a scientific basis for urban block design and offers practical implications for improving block thermal comfort.

10.1016/j.scs.2025.107044.title: Carbon emissions and their inequality in China: Insights from SHAP-based machine learning at the county level
10.1016/j.scs.2025.107044.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2025.107044.abstract: Accurate county-level carbon emission estimates are essential for achieving the "dual carbon" goals. Existing nighttime light data (NTL)-based methods often apply uniform linear coefficients, neglecting regional socioeconomic heterogeneity, while traditional regressions fail to capture nonlinear emission–driver relationships. To address the limitations, this study develops a SHAP-based machine learning framework integrating NTL and socioeconomic indicators to estimate county-level carbon emissions (CCE) from 2000–2020, and to analyze the spatiotemporal patterns, inequality, and drivers of carbon emission intensity (CEI) and per capita emissions (CEC). The results show that: (1) Compared with estimates based solely on NTL, the proposed method significantly improves the accuracy of CCE estimates. XGBoost performs best in the Eastern region (R² = 98.69%), and Random Forest performs best in the Western, Central, and Northeast regions (R² > 95%). (2) From 2000 to 2020, national emissions rose from 3.037 to 10.712 billion tonnes, with the spatial center of emissions shifting westward due to industrial relocation. Over the same period, CEI declined from 8.290 to 1.960 t/10000yuan, while CEC rose from 2.660 to 9.640 t/person. (3) Inequality in CCE and CEI narrowed, whereas CEC disparities widened, with the greatest divergence observed between the Eastern and Western regions. Variations in per capita income emerged as a key driver of unequal carbon emissions. (4) Multi-pathway decomposition reveals strong regional divergence: carbon emissions in the Central and Western regions are mainly driven by demand expansion; Eastern decarbonization is dominated by structural transitions; and in the Northeast, population loss and industrial contraction reduce demand effects, reversing urbanization’s impact on CEI after 2010. This study enhances county-level emission estimation and identifies region-specific drivers, providing scientific support for differentiated mitigation strategies and carbon market development.

10.1016/j.scs.2025.107078.title: How do built environment factors influence urban heat islands across local climate zones? Evidence from an interpretable XGBoost-SHAP model
10.1016/j.scs.2025.107078.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2025.107078.abstract: Urban heat islands (UHIs), shaped by both two-dimensional land-cover patterns and three-dimensional urban morphology, pose growing challenges to public health and energy systems. This study investigates microclimate variations in 16 residential areas of Xi’an using synchronous, high-temporal-resolution measurements from 105 sampling points. We develop an LCZ-based spatial machine-learning framework integrating XGBoost and SHAP to quantify the nonlinear impacts of built-environment indicators on near-surface temperature, humidity, and heat index. Results reveal a clear hierarchy of influence, with three-dimensional morphological indicators exerting the strongest effects, followed by landscape-ecological and two-dimensional morphological indicators. Among all variables, NDVI, sky view factor (SVF), building density (SDH), and street compactness (SCD) contribute most to microclimate regulation. Within the LCZ framework, we further identify pronounced spatial heterogeneity in thermal responses across different urban forms. Distinct synergistic interactions are also observed: substantial cooling and humidifying effects occur when NDVI > 0.3 and SVF > 0.3, while blocks characterized by low SCD (< 0.06) and high SDH (> 20) exhibit clear heat-mitigation responses. By combining detailed LCZ information, in-situ observations, and explainable machine learning, this study provides quantitative evidence linking specific morphological configurations to thermal performance and offers a transferable, climate-responsive planning framework for high-density residential environments.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107117.title: AI-integrated framework for green space optimization and air quality improvement: a futuristic approach toward sustainable urban development
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107117.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107117.abstract: Air pollution remains a critical concern in rapidly urbanizing cities, where accelerated development and the uneven distribution and limited accessibility of green spaces exacerbate environmental challenges. Although urban green spaces can mitigate pollution, their effectiveness is often constrained by inadequate planning and management strategies. To address these issues, this study proposes a multi-stage, scenario-driven green space optimization framework that applies data-driven modeling approaches to spatially assess and maximize pollutant-specific air quality benefits. The proposed methodology integrates remote sensing data, classification algorithms, vegetation indices, and hyperspectral and bioclimatic indicators to assess canopy health, structural characteristics, and guide species-level tree selection. Additionally, a GIS-based decision support system was developed to enable real-time, adaptive urban planning using sensor-linked air quality data. To validate the framework, a comprehensive case study was conducted in Hangzhou, China from 2014 to 2024, evaluating air quality, vegetation health, and key environmental drivers to promote sustainable urban development. The results demonstrated significant reductions in CO, PM2.5, PM10, NO2, and SO2 across most regions, while a slight increase in O3 was observed, highlighting the complex dynamics of secondary pollutants. The Random Forest–based optimisation framework reveals a nonlinear response of pollutant concentrations to NDVI–LAI enhancement, with PM2.5 and PM10 showing the most spatially coherent reductions under +10–20 % greening, while gaseous pollutants exhibit weaker, spatially heterogeneous responses; temporal quadrant analysis further indicates sustained-improvement dominance for NO2 and SO2, contrasted by greater instability and trade-off behaviour for O3 and PM10. The novelty of this study lies in introducing an AI-based optimization framework that leverages machine learning and spatial–temporal diagnostics to identify where and how urban green spaces can most effectively reduce different air pollutants, offering a practical decision-support approach beyond traditional correlation analyses. Future research should emphasize practical implementation by incorporating socioeconomic, health, and accessibility metrics to support the development of sustainable cities and a climate-resilient society.

10.1016/j.scs.2025.107100.title: Understanding nonlinear and spatially heterogeneous effects of urban residential morphology on land surface temperature: Integrating SOM, XGBoost-SHAP, and GWR models
10.1016/j.scs.2025.107100.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2025.107100.abstract: The thermal environment of urban residential areas significantly impacts thermal comfort and urban sustainability. However, challenges remain in accurately identifying distinct residential morphology types and in elucidating the nonlinear relationships and spatial heterogeneity between internal structure and land surface temperature (LST). This study focuses on Beijing's Haidian District, where a novel morphological classification framework was developed by integrating Local Climate Zone (LCZ) with the Self-Organizing Map (SOM) method, enabling a refined identification of residential morphology. An interpretable XGBoost-SHAP machine learning model was employed to quantify the effects of morphological factors on LST at both global and group levels. Finally, spatial heterogeneity was examined using Geographically Weighted Regression (GWR). The results indicate that (1) A total of 25 distinct urban morphology types were identified, dominated by compact and open mid-rise mixed building types (LCZ2-M and LCZ5-M), with an overall circling development. (2) In summer, compact built types exert stronger negative effects on the thermal environment than land cover types. Conversely, the opposite pattern is observed in winter. In the same LCZ, mixed layouts contribute the highest summer LST, whereas enclosed layouts dominate in winter. (3) Impervious surface fraction (ISF) emerged as the most influential factor on summer LST, followed by average building height (ABH), building density (BD), and Shannon Diversity Index (SHDI), underscoring the crucial roles of vertical spatial structure and landscape diversity. (4) The regulatory mechanisms of LST vary structurally and seasonally across different LCZ types. High-rise compact types mitigate heat accumulation through shading and ventilation, whereas open and vegetation-dominated types alleviate thermal stress via blue-green spaces evapotranspiration. Notably, open enclosure layouts provide effective shading during summer and enhance heat retention in winter. These findings offer nuanced strategies for optimizing thermal regulation within residential environments.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107134.title: Residential-ECG: AI-driven one-step generation of low-energy residential floor plans
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107134.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107134.abstract: Energy-efficient residential design plays a critical role in mitigating urban energy consumption and carbon emissions, aligning with global sustainability goals. However, existing AI-driven generative models for residential floor plans primarily focus on geometric and spatial layout while overlooking energy performance, whereas conventional building performance optimization, though effective, requires extensive computational resources, limiting their applicability in large-scale urban planning. To address this gap, we propose Residential-ECG, an AI-driven framework for one-step generation of low-energy residential floor plans, integrating energy efficiency directly into the early-stage design. Our approach consists of three components: 1) Energy Consumption Prediction Model (R-EPM), trained on 71,125 residential plans and achieving an R² value above 0.99; 2) Low-Energy Residential Floor Plan Dataset (LE-RD), the first dataset exclusively comprising 300,000 low-energy floor plans, generated via FloorplanDiffusion and screened by R-EPM, demonstrating an average energy reduction of 15.1% compared to real-world layouts; and 3) Low-Energy Residential Floor Plan Generation Model (Residential-ECG), trained on LE-RD and allowing one-step generation of high-quality, energy-efficient residential plans using outer contour and room number as inputs. Experiments show that under identical input conditions, Residential-ECG reduces energy consumption by 15.5% for 2-bedroom layouts and 15.3% for 3-bedroom layouts compared to state-of-the-art generative models. This demonstrates that AI-assisted energy-conscious design can effectively support urban sustainability and facilitate the development of affordable, low-carbon housing without imposing additional costs for advanced materials or equipment. Our approach provides a scalable, computationally accessible solution for architects, urban planners, and policymakers to accelerate the transition toward sustainable cities and societies.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107145.title: Machine learning and causal attribution of urban heat in the Phoenix metropolitan
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107145.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107145.abstract: Exacerbated thermal environment is one of the most critical challenges in urban development, which causes degradation of air quality, environmental health, and ecosystem services. While there are many existing studies of attributing urban heat to various environmental factors, the underlying causal relationship explainable by these contributors remains largely underexplored. In this study, we conducted machine learning (ML) attribution of urban heat (measured by the land surface temperature LST) to two broad categories of contributors, viz. (a) local landscape characteristics (surface albedo, vegetation coverage, building density, and measure of anthropogenic activities) and (b) meteorological conditions (precipitation, humidity, wind, pressure, solar radiation, and soil moisture), using the Phoenix metropolitan, AZ as a testbed. Furthermore, we quantified the underlying causation between these environmental factors and LST using convergent cross mapping (CCM). It was found that solar radiation and vegetation coverage (NDVI) are the two most important determinants, both statistically and causally, of urban thermal environment. We also identified the impact of water content variables (precipitation, humidity, and soil moisture) that is not captured by ML attribution but emerges as causally significant. These findings help to deepen our understanding of the underlying mechanism that regulates the urban heat and its complex interplay with other environmental factors, which, in turn, will be informative to sustainable urban planning practices.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107158.title: Integrating ensemble machine learning and SAR-based geospatial modelling for inclusive and equitable urban flood resilience
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107158.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107158.abstract: Urban flooding has become a major challenge in fast-growing cities worldwide, disrupting mobility, damaging infrastructure, and increasing social vulnerability. In Bengaluru, where rapid urban expansion and inadequate drainage exacerbate monsoon floods, this study develops an integrated and data-driven framework to map flood susceptibility and exposure between 2020 and 2025. The main objective is to generate a scientifically validated, high-resolution, and explainable flood-risk assessment model combining radar-based detection, machine learning, and social-infrastructure exposure analytics. Multi-temporal Sentinel-1 dual-polarisation (VV and VH) SAR data were used to detect flood events through backscatter change analysis, ensuring accurate mapping even under cloudy conditions. An ensemble of five algorithms-Random Forest, Histogram-based Gradient Boosting, XGBoost, Quadratic Discriminant Analysis, and Gaussian Naïve Bayes-was trained and optimized to capture complex spatial relationships between floods and controlling parameters. Explainable AI (SHAP, permutation, ablation) to identify key drivers for transparent planning. Probability calibration and reliability curves to check and correct forecast bias infrastructure and demographic overlays to quantify who and what is exposed. Results show that the ensemble delivered AUC = 0.985 with accuracy 78–83%, precision 0.78–0.83, recall 0.79–0.83, and F1 ≈ 0.80 across six independent flood events; calibration improved reliability with well-aligned predicted vs observed probabilities. Spatially, 32.63 km² were mapped as Very High and 61.73 km² as High susceptibility, with stable hotspots in Electronic City, Bommanahalli, Mahadevapura, and Bellandur-Varthur. Road exposure was dominated by local streets (62,402 segments) and tertiary roads (3505 segments), indicating neighbourhood-scale disruption; female and schedule caste (SC) populations showed disproportional exposure in central/eastern wards, while schedule tribe (ST) exposure was lower but non-negligible on the periphery. This analysis enable ward-wise prioritisation of drain upgrades, permeable retrofits, safe-route planning, and targeted protection of at-risk groups, aligning with the Sendai Framework and sustainable development goals (SDG)-11/13.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107165.title: Analyzing the impact of urban morphology on urban land surface temperature from the perspective of spatial configuration and explainable machine learning: A case study of seven cities
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107165.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107165.abstract: Urbanization has led to frequent heatwaves and urban heat islands (UHIs). While the impact of building density and other factors on land surface temperature (LST) has been studied, the mechanisms of spatial configuration remain unclear. We conducted a comparative study across seven cities (Beijing, Hangzhou, Nanjing, Shanghai, Wuhan, Zhengzhou and Changsha), integrating summer LST data with multidimensional morphological indicators. We applied both linear and machine learning models, and used SHAP (Shapley Additive exPlanations) to interpret the contribution and thresholds of variables. The results show that incorporating spatial configuration significantly improves explanatory power, and machine learning outperforms linear models. High-intensity development generally increases LST, while vegetation and mixed land use reduce LST, both exhibiting threshold effects: tree canopy cover beyond approximately 15% shows diminishing marginal cooling effects, and proximity to water bodies within 300 meters creates significant cooling (cold island) effects. Spatial configuration has a critical and nonlinear influence on LST, offering an evidence base for multidimensional, synergistic heat island mitigation and urban planning decisions.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107169.title: Decentralized off-grid vehicle-to-building (V2B) operation: A reinforcement learning approach for optimal charge–discharge control of energy storage systems
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107169.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107169.abstract: Recent advances in vehicle-to-everything (V2X) technology position electric-vehicle (EV) batteries as mobile energy-storage systems (ESSs), promising a new paradigm for power supply flexibility. However, prevailing centralized V2X operation scenarios and dynamic compensation schemes offer limited economic incentives for EV owners, hindering large-scale adoption. This study proposes a decentralized V2X scenario that treats EV owners as independent economic agents. It introduces a predetermined discharge tariff set at 70% of the contemporaneous time-of-use (ToU) electricity price, thereby offering clear, ex-ante profit expectations for all participants. Participations in V2X transactions are modeled as a time-dependent Poisson process. Within the proposed framework, we formulate an optimal ESS scheduling problem that minimizes the sum of electricity costs and ESS degradation costs for a commercial building equipped with photovoltaic (PV) generation, stationary ESS, and vehicle-to-building (V2B) interfaces. To solve this problem, we develop a world models-based reinforcement learning framework that performs multi-horizon forecasting of PV output and building load, using these forecasts as states to learn an optimal control policy. Compared with benchmark strategies, the proposed approach achieves a total cost reduction of up to 9.65% and attains near-global performance—within 1.57% of the optimality gap from the ideal strategy derived from perfect foresight data.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107196.title: An LLM-driven estimation framework for estimating regional travel structures based on spatiotemporal multi-modal travel data
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107196.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107196.abstract: Accurately characterizing regional travel structures (the distribution of travel modes) is essential for developing targeted interventions to promote green mobility and inform sustainable urban policies. However, despite considerable emphasis on optimizing regional travel structures to promote sustainable urban development, existing methods frequently overlook crucial aspects such as spatial heterogeneity and dynamic travel behaviors, limiting their effectiveness in guiding adaptive urban planning strategies. To address this gap, this study proposes a novel framework based on a fine-tuned large language model (LLM) to estimate regional travel structures. By transforming multimodal data, the task is reformulated as a text-to-text estimation problem using Llama3, enhanced through domain knowledge and chain-of-thought prompting. Applied to 335 street-level units in Beijing, the proposed model significantly improves estimation accuracy, reducing RMSE and MAE by 18%–25% compared to baseline methods. The results uncover distinct spatial patterns, with core districts heavily reliant on public transit, whereas suburban regions show greater dependence on private cars. The proposed framework shows advanced AI’s potential to offer interpretable and precise decision-support tools for optimizing urban transportation systems.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107193.title: Modeling the synergistic impact of intelligent transport systems and citizen engagement on urban outcomes: A simulation-based analysis using artificial neural networks
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107193.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107193.abstract: This study shows the synergistic effects of Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITS) and citizen engagement on key urban outcomes—namely, traffic congestion, air quality, and economic activity—within the context of smart city development. While conceptual links between smart transportation and urban performance are acknowledged, quantitative analyses of the interplay between technological infrastructure and social factors remain scarce. We developed a simulation-based approach using an Artificial Neural Network (ANN) model trained on a synthetically generated dataset comprising over 50 scenarios that represent varying levels of ITS implementation and citizen engagement (0–100%). The ANN architecture consisted of two input neurons, one hidden layer with five neurons, and three output neurons, which was validated through k-fold cross-validation.
