Results demonstrate positive synergies: both factors contribute to improvements, but citizen engagement has a disproportionately strong influence on air quality and economic activity. Sensitivity analysis confirms the robustness, while a comparison with linear regression validates the ANN's superior performance in capturing nonlinear relationships. We propose specific target thresholds for planners and discuss implications for sustainable urban mobility, particularly in developing contexts where rapid urbanization demands efficient resource allocation. The study concludes that smart transportation policies must couple technological deployment with robust community participation strategies to maximize urban outcomes. The results show significant synergistic effects, as the ANN model achieved high predictive accuracy (R²: 0.92, 0.89, 0.85) and suggest a potential inflection point near 60% citizen engagement, beyond which the simulated economic and environmental benefits accelerate more markedly.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107203.title: Context-sensitive analysis of disaster resilience and equity through geospatial explainable machine learning
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107203.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107203.abstract: Recurrent hurricanes pose significant challenges for disaster resilience and equitable recovery, yet there is limited research focusing on examining equity’s role in resilience across multiple, temporally distinct disasters. To address this gap, our study analyzes Florida communities impacted sequentially by Hurricanes Irma (2017) and Ian (2022), using FEMA Individual Assistance declarations to delineate the overlapping disaster zones. Leveraging geo-information embedded explainable machine learning, which integrates spatially explicit relationships into machine learning frameworks, we explored the interplay between disaster equity and disaster resilience. Specifically, we examined how (1) place-based equity, measured by building code standards, hazard exposure, and building conditions, and (2) capacity-based equity, measured by socioeconomic and demographic factors, influence three critical dimensions of resilience: disaster impact containment, resource mobilization, and recovery capability. Additionally, we assessed how these relationships and the relative influence of equity determinants change between the two hurricane events. This research contributes to the body of knowledge on community resilience by providing new insights into the dynamics of resilience-equity interactions across communities experiencing recurrent disasters. The findings offer actionable guidance for designing context-sensitive disaster management strategies for disaster-prone communities.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107166.title: A multi-agent system for neighborhood-scale carbon simulation: Integrating intelligent multi-source sensing with interaction-driven modeling
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107166.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107166.abstract: Excessive carbon emissions pose a major barrier to sustainable urban development; however, neighborhood-scale assessments are often hindered by data scarcity and low resolution, limiting the ability to explain how human activities and environmental factors jointly shape emissions. This study develops a neighborhood-scale carbon emissions simulation framework that integrates unmanned aerial vehicle-based remote sensing, computer vision, geographic information system techniques, and field surveys to acquire multi-source data. A multi-agent system was constructed to represent human behavior, built environments, and climate conditions as interacting agents with heterogeneous attributes and behavioral rules, enabling interaction-driven emissions estimation. A case study in Nanjing, China, estimated annual carbon emissions of 2.61 × 108 kg CO2e, corresponding to a land-based emission intensity of 106.53 kgCO2e/m2. The results reveal detailed spatiotemporal emission patterns and pronounced seasonal variability: buildings dominate emissions, mobility contributes 1.6%, and open spaces act as a net sink, offsetting over 2% of neighborhood emissions. Seasonally, summer emissions were approximately 40% higher than those in the transitional seasons, primarily driven by extended cooling operations and climate-sensitive behavioral shifts. The proposed approach advances explanatory power and computational efficiency in neighborhood-scale carbon accounting, providing a practical basis for low-carbon neighborhood management and sustainable urban development.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107199.title: Urban village recognition based on multimodal data fusion with an interpretable graph neural network
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107199.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107199.abstract: Recognition of urban villages (UVs) is of strategic importance for urban sustainable development. Existing studies mostly rely on visual information or statistics data, ignore the spatial relationship between regions and the complementarity of multimodal data, and lack the analysis of the importance of drivers. Therefore, this study integrates multimodal data, including remote sensing imageries, street view images, geographic big data, and building footprint data, and constructs both two- and three-dimensional features system that fuses visual perception, socio-economic factors, and urban morphology. A UV recognition model is developed using a graph neural network-based GraphSAGE with city blocks as graph nodes and spatial adjacencies as edges, and the GNNExplainer is introduced to analyze node importance and explain graph structure. Results showed 225 identified UVs totaling 61.4 km² in Nanjing, a representative high-density megacity in China, with an obvious ring-structured spatial distribution pattern containing 29.8 % in the core area. Recognition accuracy reached 97.2 %, which was 12.3 % and 5.1 % higher than the unimodal data and node ablation models on average, verifying the synergistic effect of visual, socio-economic, and morphological features, and the complementarity between self and neighbor node information. Cross-domain experiments in Changzhou and Suzhou cities identified 101 and 171 UVs with accuracies of 94.7 % and 92.4 %, demonstrating the model transferability. Moreover, explainability analysis revealed that high floor area ratio, high space congestion, high proportion of old buildings, and specific point-of-interest distribution patterns were typical UV characteristics. The proposed framework can provide efficient scientific support for urban planning and renewal decision-making.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107213.title: Integrating machine learning and interval fuzzy AHP for assessing metro station resilience to urban flooding
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107213.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107213.abstract: Under the dual pressures of climate change and urbanization, increasing extreme rainfall events pose significant challenges to the operation and management of urban metro systems. This study develops a multi-source, phased resilience indicator system to describe key resilient characteristics of the metro network. A novel quantitative framework called PU-IFAHP-KMEANS is developed by integrating Positive-Unlabeled (PU) learning, Interval Fuzzy Analytical Hierarchy Process (IFAHP), and K-means clustering, aiming to comprehensively assess metro station resilience under extreme rainfall conditions. The proposed PU-IFAHP-KMEANS is applied to the Shanghai metro network, evaluating resilience across three dimensions: pre-disaster flood risk prediction, vulnerability during disasters, and post-disaster recovery. By combining these three dimensions, the resilience levels of metro stations to flood disasters can be precisely quantified and visualized through Geographic Information System (GIS). Several key findings are revealed: (i) High-resilience metro stations are typically located in the suburbs of Shanghai, while low-resilience stations are mostly concentrated in the downtown areas; and (ii) Key factors such as Point of Interest (POI) density, maximum hourly rainfall, and betweenness centrality significantly impact resilience levels. Moreover, comparative experiments demonstrate that PU-IFAHP-KMEANS reduces subjectivity and uncertainty from expert input while demonstrating strong adaptability to varying rainfall scenarios. Practically, PU-IFAHP-KMEANS offers practical utility in identifying at-risk stations and enhancing targeted flood mitigation and emergency response strategies, thereby advancing the resilience of metro systems in the face of intensifying climatic extremes.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107211.title: Citizen science coupled with machine learning to quantify green-blue infrastructure cooling potential in Maricopa County, Arizona
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107211.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107211.abstract: This study investigates the spatiotemporal cooling performance of green and blue infrastructure (GBI) in the Dobson Ranch urban neighborhood in Phoenix, Arizona. We leveraged citizen science near-surface (2 m) air temperature (Tair) measurements to train a highly accurate Tair predicting LightGBM machine learning model (R2: 0.986, MAE: 0.251 °C, RMSE: 0.585 °C). On June 16, 2024, the park area exhibited approximately 1 °C cooling effect (relative to the neighborhood mean) during both day and night. In contrast, the nearby artificial lake exhibited a stronger cooling effect of 2.4 °C during the day but a slight warming of 0.3 °C at night. At 00:00, locations 50 m downwind of the park were 0.3 °C warmer than the park, while locations 50 m upwind were 0.8 °C warmer. At 11:00, we observed that the downwind area is 0.8 °C cooler and the upwind area is 0.6 °C warmer—at the same 50 m distances relative to the park. We also observed 1 °C cooler and warmer effects respectively at the same 50 m downwind and upwind locations at 19:00 on June 17, 2024. Our data-driven analysis highlights potential limitations of car-traverse measurements, showing that failure to account for temporal variations during the traverse can lead to overestimation of Tair at night and underestimation during the day. Our analysis also showed only a weak correlation (coefficient: 0.48) between Landsat-derived land surface temperature (LST) and model predicted Tair at the time of the local Landsat overpass (∼11.00). This highlights the potential error of relying solely on LST for human thermal exposure analysis—particularly within the heterogenous built-environment.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107239.title: Uncovering the foundation-capacity-performance logic of urban resilience: Identifying dynamic weights and nonlinear relationships through a spatial machine learning framework
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107239.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107239.abstract: Urban resilience has emerged as a critical topic in urban planning and spatial governance amidst rapid urbanization and increasing climatic uncertainty. However, the structural relationships, functional interactions, and temporal coupling among the multidimensional attributes of resilience remain insufficiently understood. To address this gap, this study introduces a Foundation-Capacity-Performance (FCP) model that links the foundational conditions, adaptive mechanisms, and spatial expressions of resilience, and develops a dynamic weighting framework integrating random forest, geographically weighted regression, and TOPSIS to capture nonlinear effects, spatial heterogeneity, and temporal consistency. Using multi-source raster data for the central urban area of Nanjing from 2005 to 2020, we quantify an overall urban resilience index and map the results onto the foundational and capacity dimensions. The results indicate that: (1) urban resilience in Nanjing increased steadily from 2005 to 2020, exhibiting a networked diffusion pattern from core districts toward near-suburban and peripheral areas; (2) early improvements were primarily driven by infrastructure robustness and system recovery, whereas later enhancement stemmed from more balanced social services, functional diversification, and ecological network optimization; (3) Key indicators (e.g., population density, built-up intensity, and connectivity) display notable nonlinear effects within threshold ranges, while ecological attributes maintain consistently positive effects; and (4) the proposed dynamic weighting model substantially outperforms static schemes in temporal consistency and interannual prediction. Overall, this study provides a coherent theoretical framework and methodological pathway for multi-period, multi-scale resilience assessment, offering quantitative evidence to support resilience-oriented urban planning and governance.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107255.title: Neural network-enhanced BIM framework for designing thermally comfortable urban environments
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107255.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107255.abstract: Outdoor thermal comfort (OTC) evaluation during the design phase is often compromised by the computational complexity of physical simulations. Consequently, current BIM-integrated workflows predominantly rely on simplified proxies, assuming surface temperature equals air temperature. This study hypothesizes that such simplifications introduce significant errors in long-wave radiation calculations, thereby distorting thermal comfort assessments. To address this, we present a computational framework that integrates a physics-based surrogate model (ESMUST), trained on 42 million EnergyPlus datasets, into the BIM environment. Unlike conventional methods, this framework predicts surface temperatures based on thermodynamic principles. A comparative analysis conducted on a university campus demonstrated that the proposed method captures surface temperature variations that proxy-based approaches inherently cannot represent. The results indicate that explicit surface temperature modeling alters the calculated COMFA thermal budget by 22.5–25.1 W/m2, a magnitude sufficient to shift thermal comfort classifications and influence design decision-making. Comparative validation with ENVI-met simulations confirmed consistent thermal comfort improvement patterns, with the proposed framework achieving computational times approximately two orders of magnitude faster. This research demonstrates the necessity of physics-based surface temperature modeling in BIM-integrated thermal comfort assessment and provides a computationally efficient methodology for early-stage design evaluation.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107253.title: Dynamic simulation of urban agglomeration network resilience under disturbances: An integrated deep learning and agent-based approach – Case study of the Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei region
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107253.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107253.abstract: The development of resilient urban agglomerations is a strategic imperative for regional security and sustainable development. However, existing static evaluations often fail to capture the spatio-temporal qualitative dependencies among network nodes and the reciprocal interactions between multi-agent decision-making and network evolution. To bridge these gaps, this study proposes a GAT-ABM framework integrating Entropy-CRITIC weighting, Graph Attention Networks (GAT), and Agent-Based Modeling (ABM). Using the Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei Urban Agglomeration (BTHUA) as a case study, we construct a multidimensional resilience index and simulate network dynamics under extreme disturbances. The results reveal: (1) marked core-periphery disparities, with central cities exhibiting resilience 1.2–2.5 times higher than peripheral ones; (2) high network sensitivity, where 57.8 % of secondary nodes fluctuate significantly (>25 %) under connection strength variations; and (3) a phased recovery mechanism where enterprise response reduces initial impacts, government intervention accelerates mid-term recovery by 60.9 %, and public participation drives 74.4 % of post-disaster reconstruction. By quantifying the interplay between agent behaviors and network structural shifts, this study provides a dynamic tool for policymakers to optimize cross-city risk governance and regional collaborative resilience.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107261.title: Data-driven urban mobility planning: A GIS-based spatial modeling approach for shared mobility hub placement
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107261.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107261.abstract: Strategically planned shared mobility hubs are critical for enhancing multimodal integration, reducing car dependency, and supporting sustainable urban transportation systems. This study proposes a robust GIS-based multi-criteria decision-support framework to identify optimal locations for shared mobility hubs in İzmir, Türkiye. The framework integrates 18 spatial indicators capturing micromobility trip demand, public transportation and cycling accessibility, land-use intensity, urban activity concentration, and traffic safety conditions. To enhance methodological rigor and robustness, two fundamentally different weighting philosophies were implemented: i.) an expert-driven Fuzzy Analytic Hierarchy Process (Fuzzy-AHP), and ii.) a data-driven Entropy-TOPSIS model. The two models produced independent suitability surfaces reflecting contrasting but complementary planning logics. The results indicated that Fuzzy-AHP approach favored locations with established micromobility demand and continuous cycling infrastructure, particularly along the İzmir Gulf coastline and university districts, whereas Entropy-TOPSIS emphasized emerging opportunity areas characterized by heterogeneous public transport accessibility and a high concentration of points of interests (POIs). These outputs were integrated through a novel Integrated Suitability Index (ISI), enabling systematic comparison and reducing method-specific bias. Using an 80% ISI threshold, followed by spatial clustering, 21 high-priority shared mobility hub locations were identified. All selected hubs lie within overlapping high-suitability zones of both models, demonstrating strong cross-model consistency and structural robustness. Overall, the findings confirm that combining expert knowledge with data-driven variability substantially strengthens spatial decision-making for shared mobility hub placement. The proposed framework provides actionable guidance for urban planners and policymakers and offers a scalable decision-support tool for advancing resilient, user-centered, and integrated multimodal transportation systems.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107299.title: A spatio-temporal graph convolutional networks framework for urban fire risk management and resource optimization
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107299.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107299.abstract: This study proposes a multi-scale Spatio-Temporal Graph Convolutional Network (ST-GCN) framework for dynamic subdistrict-level fire risk prediction in Wuhan, China. By integrating meteorological data, built environment features, and urban function data into a graph structure, the model effectively captures complex spatiotemporal dependencies. A weighted loss function is employed to address fire data imbalance. Results demonstrate that the framework achieves AUC values of 0.735, 0.769, and 0.857 for short-, medium-, and long-term predictions, respectively, outperforming baseline models by 8.6%–26.8%. Explainability analysis identifies building age, population density, and commercial activity as primary risk drivers, while climatic factors proved less significant than anthropogenic activities in this urban context. Crucially, the study reveals a severe spatial mismatch, with only 41.41% of subdistricts meeting the 5-minute firefighting response standard. Simulation results indicate that expanding the effective service radius is superior to equipment upgrades, potentially increasing coverage to 62.12%. This research provides a scientifically grounded tool for proactive risk management and quantitative insights for optimizing urban resilience.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107272.title: AI-driven urban evolution forecasting: A unified memory-aware multi-conditional generation framework for sustainable development planning
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107272.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107272.abstract: Sustainable urban development requires predictive models that can comprehensively integrate multiple interdependent factors such as building density, height distribution, transportation networks, and historical evolution to support evidence-based planning. However, existing AI-based generative models cannot effectively integrate these factors, resulting in fragmented predictions that fail to support comprehensive urban planning strategies. To solve these issues, we propose MMCN (Memory-aware Multi-Conditional generation Network), an AI-driven framework that enables planners to forecast urban layout evolution by comprehensively modeling the complex interactions among multiple urban development factors. MMCN addresses three critical planning challenges through technical innovations: (1) a multi-conditional control architecture that processes building density, height, and transportation factors as interconnected elements influencing sustainable urban form; (2) a spatial continuity mechanism that ensures generated layouts maintain regional coherence; and (3) a temporal consistency framework that leverages historical layout patterns to capture long-term evolution trends. Using a comprehensive urban evolution dataset of Shenzhen, we demonstrate that MMCN substantially improves forecasting accuracy and spatial coherence, achieving an SSIM of 0.885 and a Boundary IoU of 0.642, significantly outperforming all baseline models. This work provides technical support for urban planning practitioners in sustainable development scenario analysis, enabling the formulation of long-term planning decisions that can balance urban growth with sustainability objectives and support the achievement of sustainable urban development goals.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107262.title: From mature to emerging cities: Cross-city transfer of grid-level EV charging station prioritization via Domain-adversarial neural networks
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107262.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107262.abstract: Electrification is accelerating, making the questions of where and when to deploy EV charging infrastructure urgent. Existing studies are predominantly single-city and lack temporal labels that capture build-out rhythm, limiting generalization to emerging cities. We develop a cross-city transfer learning framework that first clusters Chinese cities by climate and geography and restricts transfer to within-cluster pairs. Within the typology, we evaluate the framework on two representative transfer pairs, Shenzhen→Dongguan and Beijing→Zhengzhou, involving cities of similar type but contrasting development levels. Robustness is verified across grid resolutions (200/500/700 m), confirming 500 m as an optimal balance. Using multi-source urban features on 500-m grids and a five-level deployment-urgency label derived from multi-year build-out, we train a Domain-Adversarial Neural Network (DANN) to predict grid-level prioritization and validate externally at city and street-sample scales. The framework outperforms baselines in cross-city transfer (≈8% Macro-F1 gain); under a Top-10% budget, it captures over 60% of next-year additions with an average nearest distance <500 m, and high-priority grids co-locate along transport spines and public/commercial corridors. The resulting reproducible pipeline—national heterogeneity→clustering prior→adversarial transfer →dual-scale validation—supports spatial prioritization and shortlist screening for EV charger deployment in emerging cities; broader validation on more diverse city pairs remains future work.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107319.title: The relationship between building and urban mobility-based energy consumption and urban form: A machine learning approach
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107319.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107319.abstract: Urban energy consumption studies predominantly focus on building energy use. However, urban form has the potential to influence energy consumption not only through building morphology but also through mobility demands shaped by spatial location within the city. In different locational contexts such as central, peripheral, coastal, and transitional zones, urban form varies in terms of density, building layout, and accessibility, which affects both building-related and trip-related energy demand. Despite this, studies that jointly evaluate the combined effects of urban morphological characteristics and locational mobility dynamics on energy consumption remain limited. Addressing this gap, this study assumes that urban energy consumption should be examined not only at the building scale but also in an integrated manner with the locational characteristics of urban form. Within this framework, urban forms in Istanbul were classified into seven categories using the k-means clustering algorithm. Subsequently, a dataset consisting of morphological variables derived from 32,112 buildings was modeled to predict building energy consumption. Among ten machine learning techniques, Random Forest was identified as the most successful algorithm, achieving an R² value of 0.87. The effects of urban morphological variables were interpreted using SHapley Additive Explanations. In the next step, energy consumption resulting from trips between Traffic Analysis Zones across different transportation modes was calculated. When building-related and trip-related energy consumption were evaluated together, Open low rise was identified as the least efficient form with an average energy consumption of 186 kWh/year·m², while Open skyscraper was identified as the most efficient form with an average of 85 kWh/year·m². However, when areas dominated by building energy and those dominated by trip-related energy were examined, it was observed that the energy performance of urban forms varied depending on spatial context. The findings provide insights to inform energy-oriented urban planning and urban design approaches.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107312.title: Mapping diurnal urban heat dynamics in data-scarce global south cities: A machine learning-enabled diagnostic framework applied to Kabul
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107312.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107312.abstract: Urbanization in the Global South is accelerating at an unprecedented pace, heightening vulnerability to the surface urban heat island (SUHI) effect amid limited in-situ monitoring and fragmented long-term urban datasets at neighborhood-scale resolution. This study addresses these challenges by applying a replicable machine learning-enabled diagnostic framework to analyze long-term SUHI dynamics, using Kabul—a high-altitude, semi-arid city with rapid, uneven, and informal urbanization—as a representative case. By integrating multi-satellite datasets and geospatial analytics on Google Earth Engine, we generate spatially consistent diurnal land surface temperature (LST) maps at 30 m resolution for 2000–2020, providing a detailed characterization of diurnal surface temperature patterns across settlement types in similar contexts. The application of Gradient Boosting Regression (GBR), Quantile Regression (QR), and spatial autocorrelation analysis revealed trends and typological differences in LST between formal and informal areas. The average difference between the temperatures of day and night decreased from around 25 °C in 2000 to about 17 °C in 2020, indicating reduced daytime extremes alongside persistent nocturnal warmth. Spatial clustering weakened over time, becoming more fragmented, signifying a shift from a purely central to a polycentric SUHI pattern. Informal settlements generally recorded higher daytime LST values, particularly in the upper quantile τ = 0.9, while formal areas exhibited stronger nocturnal heat retention. The study demonstrates how a settlement-integrated remote sensing workflow can reveal diurnal thermal disparities and long-term spatial reorganization of surface heat in cities with limited ground observations. These insights support context-sensitive heat adaptation strategies for rapidly urbanizing, semi-arid cities facing uneven heat impacts across socio-spatial landscapes.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107306.title: Urban polycentricity, spatial compactness, and carbon emission efficiency in China: An ensemble machine learning evaluation
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107306.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107306.abstract: Cities, as hubs of economic activity, technological innovation, and population concentration, are both significant sources of carbon emissions and critical stakeholders in climate mitigation. Improving carbon emission efficiency (CEE) has become a central focus in advancing low-carbon urban development. This study examines the relationships among urban polycentricity, spatial compactness, and CEE, using panel data from 275 prefecture-level cities in China from 2006 to 2019. The analysis applies the Non-Radial Directional Distance Function (NDDF) to measure CEE. It integrates ensemble machine learning methods, including Random Forest (RF), Gradient Boosting Regression Tree (GBRT), Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP), and Accumulated Local Effects (ALE). The findings reveal nonlinear and spatiotemporally dynamic links between urban form and carbon performance. A stage-dependent pattern emerges: moderately polycentric and compact urban structures enhance CEE, while excessive expansion and high polycentricity reduce it. Economic and population density promote CEE up to a threshold, after which the effect weakens. Industrial SO₂ emissions consistently hinder CEE. Regional differences are pronounced. In eastern China, economic growth, industrial emissions, and population density dominate CEE outcomes. In central and western regions, topography and urbanization rates play stronger roles. Across all city clusters, economic development and industrial SO₂ emissions remain key determinants of CEE. City size also matters. Medium and small cities benefit the most from polycentric development, while large cities should prioritize economic restructuring and pollution control. By integrating urban polycentricity, spatial compactness and carbon emission efficiency into a data-driven, interpretable framework, this study provides empirical evidence and practical insights to guide urban low-carbon strategies that align with China’s dual-carbon goals and global climate commitments.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107342.title: Collaboratively optimize of multi-scale spatial form within urban blocks for low-carbon performance: A machine learning-driven design support framework
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107342.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107342.abstract: Achieving carbon-neutral city goals requires leveraging performance-based design in the early stages of planning. However, performance-driven multi-scale spatial form optimization for building carbon emissions has not yet been fully investigated. This disconnect presents a critical barrier to developing sustainable urban blocks. To bridge this gap, this study develops and validates a machine learning-driven framework to support the collaborative optimization of multi-scale spatial form for superior carbon performance. Taking office blocks in Wuhan as a case study, a parametric model was developed based on 50 real-world examples to ensure linked changes in spatial form of block and building scale. This model was used to generate a large dataset for training ensemble learning algorithms to rapidly predict and balance three key sustainability indicators: building energy carbon emissions (BECE), solar energy carbon reduction (SECR), and net carbon emissions (NCE). The framework demonstrates significant potential, compared with the simulation method, the proposed method can accelerate 150–160 times, informed decision-making for planners. The resulting optimized design solutions achieved an average 11.53 % reduction in BECE and an 79.34 % reduction in NCE compared to initial schemes. Using explainable AI (SHAP), the analysis overcomes the "black box" problem of machine learning models, identifying plot ratio and building density as the most critical parameters influencing net emissions and offering clear, actionable guidance for designers. This research provides a powerful, data-driven support tool for architects and urban planners to integrate carbon performance assessment into the formative stages of urban design. By offering a rapid and intelligent method for generating and evaluating low-carbon block configurations, this framework contributes directly to the creation of more sustainable, resilient, and climate-responsive cities.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107334.title: Data-driven microclimate analysis for thermal comfort optimization in arid-hot urban blocks
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107334.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107334.abstract: This research examines how climate change and urban decay impact well-being in Central Asia, focusing on Shihezi in northern Xinjiang. It assesses summertime extreme heat conditions in historic commercial areas using data from multiple sources. This study employs spatial clustering of Points of Interest (POI), field-based meteorological monitoring, subjective surveys, and microclimate modeling to evaluate of spatiotemporal variations in the outdoor thermal environment. Locally adjusted thermal comfort thresholds were established using the Universal Thermal Climate Index (UTCI) and participant feedback. The study also assesses targeted heat mitigation interventions, identifying a diurnal thermal pattern with peak heat stress occurring in the late afternoon and temperature differential of 7.6 °C between shaded and unshaded areas. Of 174 participants, 66.1% reported feeling warm or hot, 62.1% still deemed the environment acceptable. A notable negative correlation emerged between thermal and radiation preferences relative to UTCI values. The calibrated neutral UTCI was 27.2 °C, with an acceptable ranging from 19.4 °C to 28.1 °C. Simulation-based improvement scenarios indicated that substituting current trees with species possessing higher leaf area indices yielded the most effective cooling, resulting in a 4.4 °C reduction in UTCI. This study establishes a specific thermal comfort benchmark for historic commercial blocks in the hot-arid regions of Central Asia, offering a transferable, evidence-based framework for climate-resilient urban regeneration in the Eurasian arid corridor.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107330.title: One city, two heats: An LLM-enabled comparative analysis of heat perception, thermal environment, and health pathways in Beijing, China
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107330.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107330.abstract: Urbanization intensifies urban heat islands and health risks, yet most studies prioritize physical heat exposure. Emerging work notes that perceived heat can diverge from thermal measures, but rigorous comparison is limited. We address this gap by using a Large Language Mode (LLM) to extract Social Media Heat Perception (SMHP) from social-media posts about Beijing’s urban parks and integrating it with Physical Thermal Environment (PTE) derived from remote sensing and a population-weighted model. Coupled with subdistrict indicators of physical health and well-being, we apply Partial Least Squares–Structural Equation Modeling to identify direct and mediating pathways and Multiscale Geographically Weighted Regression to map spatial heterogeneity. We show that a LLM can robustly detect semantic SMHP, achieving a 94.5% true positive rate for extreme heat-discomfort cases. The results indicate that PTE is a stronger predictor of health outcomes and is shaped by macro-scale landscapes and regional context, whereas SMHP is associated with micro-scale, in-park features. The biophysical cooling effect has a greater impact on PTE than SMHP, suggesting a “perception lag” in which expressed sentiment is less responsive than objective measurements. Built and socioeconomic factors exhibit a “heat paradox,” where greater resources coincide with higher exposure. Spatial mismatches between SMHP and PTE reveal that temperature-only metrics can miss hidden vulnerabilities. We advocate a coordinated, dual-dimension, multi-scale strategy to support evidence-based climate adaptation and health equity.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107386.title: How natural–built environments shape spatiotemporal patterns of urban heat islands: Integrating water-gradient stratification and machine learning
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107386.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107386.abstract: Urban heat islands (UHI) have intensified with urban expansion and climate warming. In waterfront cities, built environments (BE) have developed in close interaction with water-related natural environments (NE), yet the role of natural–built environments (NBE) in shaping UHI spatiotemporal patterns remains unclear. This study used Wuhan as a case city and classified the entire area into six waterfront gradients (L1–L6). The dataset included a multidimensional NBE index system and land surface temperatures (LST), serving as a key indicator for UHI from 2013 to 2023. At the system level, bivariate spatial autocorrelation and geographically and temporally weighted regression (GTWR) models were employed to elucidate the spatiotemporal interactions between NBE and UHI. At the factor level, Pearson correlation and machine learning models were combined to identify multi-gradient stratified responses of key drivers. Results showed a 3.60 % decline in NE, mainly in L1–L3, and a 14.21 % increase in BE, concentrated in L3–L4. UHI was strongest in L1–L2, with LST of 35.20 °C and 35.40 °C, while L6 exhibited lower LST (32.64 °C). LST’s standard deviation ellipses aligned with the Yangtze River, but centroid shifts and hotspot evolution diverged from NE. In L6, NE showed a mitigating effect on UHI (GTWR = −0.18), while in L4, BE showed strong positive reinforcement (GTWR = 0.70). Random forest–SHAP analysis further revealed strong spatiotemporal heterogeneity in marginal contributions of NBE factors to UHI. BE factors formed synergistic warming peaks in L1–L3 with cumulative amplification over time. In L4, compensatory effects between BE and NE became stronger. In inland L5–L6 gradients, NE showed stage-dependent UHI mitigation effects, with delayed gradient responses activated when ecological thresholds exceeded 0.5. These findings provide evidence for climate-resilient planning in waterfront cities and support SDGs 11 and 13.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107355.title: Impacts of grey-green spatial patterns on carbon emissions and sequestration in expanding and shrinking cities: An explainable machine learning approach
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107355.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107355.abstract: Rapid urbanization and the rush to meet global climate commitments require a clearer understanding of how urban form drives carbon emissions (CE) and carbon sequestration (CS), here represented by net primary productivity (NPP) as a proxy for vegetation-driven carbon uptake. While existing research confirms that spatial morphology shapes CE and CS, it offers limited insight into how these relationships shift across different stages of urban development. In this study, we examine Chengdu and Harbin as representative expanding and shrinking cities and apply machine learning models integrated with Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP) to identify the nonlinear effects of grey-green spatial patterns on urban carbon dynamics. Our results show that in expanding cities, structural attributes of grey space dominate CE patterns, whereas green space coverage and connectivity play a decisive role in strengthening CS. In shrinking cities, grey space characteristics largely govern both CE and CS. We also find that expanding cities respond more strongly to variations in spatial agglomeration and grey-green morphological coupling, displaying broader and more elastic emission-reduction and sequestration-enhancement ranges, whereas shrinking cities exhibit more constrained yet stable responses. Moreover, expanding cities reveal a marked synergistic effect when agglomeration and connectivity improve simultaneously, producing concurrent declines in CE and gains in CS. These findings underscore the threshold sensitivity and city-type specificity of grey-green spatial influences on the urban carbon cycle and offer evidence-based guidance for designing differentiated spatial optimization strategies that enhance sequestration and curb emissions in cities undergoing different development trajectories.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107353.title: A machine learning-based mediation analysis of urban form influences on building energy use: evidence from Seoul, South Korea
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107353.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107353.abstract: Understanding the mechanisms through which urban contextual form influences building energy use is critical for developing accurate urban building energy models. However, few studies have examined the mechanisms that mediate the effect of urban form on building energy use. This study investigates three mediating mechanisms that link urban form to building energy use: solar insolation, contextual temperature, and occupant behavior. Using monthly energy use of residential plots in Seoul, South Korea, the study estimates mediation effects in summer and winter seasons. An artificial neural network (ANN) mediation model is trained to capture nonlinearity and interactions in the relationship and compared to traditional linear mediation models. Results suggest the ANN-based method has a higher accuracy and enhanced interpretability. Analyses show that contextual temperature is the dominant mediator for summer electricity and winter energy uses, with effects of 24-54%, while solar insolation also plays a major mediating role, with effects up to 47% in winter electricity. Occupant behavior mediates approximately 2-5% of urban form's effects on seasonal energy uses. Although modest, these effects are significant for green and water cover. Notably, significant residual effects persist for building height, and distances to green and water, especially for winter gas, indicating additional, unmodeled pathways. Partial dependence plots are used to assess the nature of the relationship. Sensitivity analyses for context size, model specifications, regularization, spatial autocorrelation, and sub-contexts are conducted, offering comparative and methodological insights. Overall, the study clarifies how urban form influences energy use, informing urban planning and energy policies.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107398.title: Hybrid deep reinforcement learning for optimizing electric vehicle charging station placement: Multi agent-based simulations using real-world data
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107398.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107398.abstract: The strategic placement of electric vehicle (EV) charging stations is essential to accelerate EV adoption and ensure sustainable urban mobility. Existing research often proposes theoretical solutions that overlook practical constraints that limit their practical impact. To bridge this gap between theory and practice, in this study we propose a new hybrid deep reinforcement learning (HDRL) framework that incorporates critical real-world operational and financial constraints to guide actionable decision-making. Our approach uses a graph neural network (GNN) to represent the road network, distances, and accessibility score data of the city in the form of a spatial graph, effectively capturing the complex interdependencies between potential station locations. This graphical representation facilitates the learning of a deep reinforcement learning (DRL) agent, which is trained to determine the optimal set of locations that maximizes station accessibility while respecting constraints. A key part of our analysis includes a comparative evaluation of the performance and cost–benefit of two common charging technologies, 22 kW and 50 kW chargers, to determine the optimal technology for the proposed infrastructure plan. In addition, we determine the ideal number of chargers for each station, which is a crucial variable that is often ignored or fixed. To ensure robustness, the results obtained are simulated in the simulation of urban mobility (SUMO) environment using real data, generating realistic usage statistics. Our results demonstrate that the proposed HDRL framework significantly outperforms traditional placement strategies when evaluated based on key metrics including average user wait times, budget allocation efficiency, charger utilization rates, and overall network accessibility. These findings offer a flexible and practical tool for reducing infrastructure investment risks and accelerating the transition to electric mobility.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107400.title: Applications and challenges of machine learning in urban thermal environment: A systematic review
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107400.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107400.abstract: The synergistic pressure of urbanization and global warming requires us to develop powerful analytical tools to interpret the complex dynamic changes in the urban thermal environment (UTE). This study adopts the PRISMA system evaluation method. Through the core database and strict literature screening process, 493 studies that meet the inclusion criteria are screened from the 3299 literatures originally retrieved. The research systematically summarizes the application status and technical characteristics of machine learning (ML) algorithm in four major subject areas: UTE prediction and simulation, urban spatial morphology research, architectural morphology analysis, and urban thermal vulnerability and thermal comfort assessment. The research results show that supervised learning (SL) (especially random forest (RF), support vector machine (SVM) and eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost)) dominates feature extraction and prediction tasks, while multi-source data such as remote sensing and land coverage are used as core inputs. Crucially, the field is undergoing a paradigm shift from a single predictive model to a comprehensive framework that integrates interpretability and optimization. Despite these advances, challenges persist in data quality, the opacity of the "black box" model, and cross-regional mobility. In order to solve these problems, this paper distills practical implementation suggestions from the aspects of computing resources, missing data processing, spatial cross-verification and uncertainty quantification, providing systematic theoretical reference and methodological guidance for researchers in the field of UTE, as well as resilient urban development, thermal risk management and sustainability.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107407.title: A Data Assimilation-Informed Deep Learning Framework for Transient Turbulent Urban Wind Field Prediction: Integrating Sparse High-Fidelity Data and Low-Resolution Simulations
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107407.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107407.abstract: Rapid and accurate prediction of wind speed fields in urban environments is vital for understanding the urban climate, promoting urban sustainability, and disaster mitigation. However, progress in this field continues to face two significant limitations, namely the substantial computational demands of computational fluid dynamics (CFD) methods, and the inherent challenge of error accumulation in deep learning approaches. To address these issues, we propose a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN)-based data assimilation model that serves as a CFD surrogate model, aiming to enhance computational efficiency while improving transient urban wind field prediction accuracy. By integrating a novel temporally enhanced hybrid U-Net architecture, the generator enables precise flow field pattern prediction. The discriminator leverages sparse high-precision data for dynamic assimilation and correction to improve the stability and accuracy of long-term predictions. The results of our experiments across multiple scenarios show that our model outperforms CFD numerical simulation methods by two orders of magnitude in efficiency, reduces the MAE and MSE by 29.2% and 38.6% respectively compared with CFD-URANS simulations, and significantly enhances turbulent flow characteristic reconstruction, thus providing a highly efficient data assimilation framework for simulating wind speed fields in urban environments.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107403.title: Exposure-Aware commuting: Geo-AI–Driven route optimization to reduce NO2 in urban road networks
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107403.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107403.abstract: Air pollution exposure during daily commuting poses significant health risks, yet most route-planning studies focus on PM₂.₅ and rely on coarse spatial interpolation methods. This study advances exposure-aware mobility by developing a high-resolution geospatial artificial intelligence (Geo-AI) framework for Kaohsiung City, Taiwan. This framework models nitrogen dioxide (NO₂), a traffic-related pollutant with sharp spatial gradients, and integrates it into an optimized route-planning system. A Light Gradient Boosting Machine Regression (LGBMR) model was trained on continuous monitoring data from December 2021 to February 2024. The model achieved robust predictive performance (R² = 0.87), enabling reliable estimates of pollutant concentrations at the street segment scale. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analysis revealed that chemical-industry density, waste-treatment facility density, and road network density were among the most influential predictors of elevated NO₂. By combining 10 × 10 m NO₂ concentration data from the model and a detailed road network database, we simulated 3000 randomized commuting routes and compared distance-optimized and exposure-optimized routing scenarios. On average, low-exposure routing reduced NO₂ exposure by 2.04%, while 259 routes achieved reductions of over 5%. In some cases, the reduction reached 39.70%. A representative 365-day commuting simulation was conducted for the entire year of 2024. It projected an annual cumulative reduction in exposure of 9.02 × 10⁵ ppb·s for a typical commuter using optimized routes. These results underscore the feasibility and public health potential of integrating high-resolution pollutant mapping with route optimization, enabling personalized, exposure-conscious mobility. It offers a scalable pathway for urban planners and policymakers to mitigate long-term health risks, especially in densely populated Asian cities with high motor vehicle use.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107413.title: Hazard-responsive digital twin for weather-driven urban resilience and affordability
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107413.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107413.abstract: Compounding weather hazards, such as wildfire-induced outages and urban heatwaves, challenge the reliability, affordability, and safety of urban services. We present a Hazard-Responsive Digital Twin (H-RDT) that combines physics-informed neural network modeling, multimodal data fusion, affiliation learning, and affordability-aware risk analytics for urban-scale response. In a screening-level synthetic district with diverse building archetypes and populations, a simulated wildfire–outage–heatwave cascade shows that H-RDT maintains stable indoor temperature predictions (∼31–33 °C peaks) under partial sensor loss, while reproducing outage-driven surges and recovery. The reinforcement learning based fusion module adaptively reweights IoT, UAV, and satellite inputs to sustain spatiotemporal coverage, and the affordability-adjusted mapping isolates high-vulnerability clusters such as schools, clinics, low-income housing. Prospective interventions, i.e., preemptive cooling-center activation and microgrid sharing, reduce population-weighted thermal risk by 11–13%, shrink the 95th-percentile (tail) risk by 7–17%, and cut overheating hours by up to 9%. Beyond this synthetic demonstration, the framework establishes a transferable pathway for real-city implementation by linking hazard modeling, reliability-focused analytics, and decision intelligence for resilience planning.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107412.title: Artificial intelligence enhanced workflow for noise conscious urban design in high density cities
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107412.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107412.abstract: Acoustic comfort becomes critical for health and the quality of life in dense metropolises, yet responses from urban planning and design are limited. Existing noise mitigation relies on regulations of urban density, street dimensions, or post-hoc diagnosis at project level, while advanced simulations are computationally intensive and not ready to be integrated into planning and design process. This study introduces a novel workflow to optimize building configurations under site constraints with the objective of reducing traffic noise exposure. The workflow employs a neural network model trained using a 3D urban noise dataset generated using an empirically validated, state-of-the-art simulation. The model was then coupled with a parametric building form generator and an evolutionary algorithm to iteratively identify optimal building configurations. The workflow was tested with a high-rise mixed-use development in Hong Kong, where results indicated reductions of average traffic noise exposure of up to 1.54 dB compared to a baseline design, and 3.53 dB compared with the least effective configuration. These noise reductions resulted from optimized building massing and spatial configurations that balance sound energy shielded by buildings with that reflected in street canyons. Analysis using gradient boosting regression and SHapley Additive exPlanations further revealed the non-linear relationships between noise exposure and parameters such as position-dependent building volume and average building height-to-distance ratio, suggesting the current noise regulations may be insufficient. The proposed workflow demonstrates potentials to inform urban planning and design practices by incorporating traffic noise exposure mitigation as a design objective.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107434.title: An AI-driven MABM–BIM–DL framework for energy consumption prediction in three representative types of urban public buildings in Wuhan
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107434.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107434.abstract: Accurate prediction of energy consumption in urban public buildings is essential for city planning and sustainable development, yet remains challenging when indoor layouts and occupant behaviors differ across building types. Taking Wuhan as the study context, this work proposes an AI-driven framework for public-building energy prediction that integrates multi-building agent-based modeling (MABM), building information modeling (BIM), and deep learning (DL) to forecast energy use in hospitals, shopping malls and office buildings. An MABM-BIM model is first developed and then calibrated and validated against one year of measured data from the three building types. The model explicitly represents the coupled processes among indoor layout, occupant behavior and energy use, and generates synthetic energy time series that are both behaviorally plausible and consistent with widely used calibration criteria. On this basis, four deep learning predictors (DNN, RNN, LSTM and Transformer) are trained on a combination of simulated and measured data and are benchmarked against a representative baseline model from the literature. Across the three building types, the proposed AI models increase R2 by 12.9%–14.0% and Accuracy by 12.2%–13.0%, while reducing MSE, MAE and MAAPE. The Transformer delivers the best overall performance, highlighting the advantage of attention-based architectures for learning long-horizon temporal dependencies and cross-feature interactions. The trained predictors can be embedded as BIM-linked modules to support rapid energy estimation in planning and conceptual design, thus enabling data-driven scheme screening and sustainability-oriented decision-making for public buildings in hot-summer and cold-winter climatic regions.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107421.title: Graph neural network actor-critic model development for smart and resilient parcel-based land use allocation
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107421.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107421.abstract: Smart city planning and urban resilience are becoming increasingly vital for creating sustainable and adaptive urban environments capable of withstanding diverse socio-economic and environmental challenges. Central to these efforts is land use allocation, which is inherently a nonlinear, multi-objective, and complex problem. When it is posed at the neighborhood scale, where localized decisions significantly influence overall urban resilience and smart city objectives, the allocation problem exhibits distinct spatial characteristics. Parcel area variation, building density assignment, and design considerations introduce additional complexity into the allocation process. Accordingly, this paper presents a multi-objective mathematical formulation of the land use allocation problem that explicitly incorporates these spatial characteristics at the neighborhood scale within the context of urban resilience and smart city planning. Subsequently, a multi-objective graph neural network actor-critic (MOGNNAC) reinforcement learning model is developed to address the proposed problem. The model leverages the ability of the MOGNNAC to capture spatial dependencies, support scalable and adaptive decision-making, and effectively handle the intricacy, nonlinearity, and high dimensionality of the formulated allocation problem. The proposed MOGNNAC framework is then implemented and evaluated against NSGA-II (Non-dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm II) and MOPSO (Multi-Objective Particle Swarm Optimization), two widely used algorithms for solving land use allocation problems. The results demonstrate that MOGNNAC not only produces competitive solutions but also provides valuable insights into developing land use allocation models that integrate resilience and smart city planning frameworks while accounting for density, design, and parcel area variations.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107457.title: Attributing the urban heat island effect to urban land use patterns with integrated machine learning and GeoShapley method
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107457.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107457.abstract: Urban land-use patterns are fundamentally associated with the Urban Heat Island (UHI) effect. However, conventional models struggle to capture the complex non-linear associations and spatial heterogeneity between land layouts and Land Surface Temperature (LST). This study characterizes these associations using high-resolution land-use data and a spatially interpretable framework integrating machine learning with the GeoShapley method. To ensure methodological robustness, a Spatial Block Cross-Validation (SBCV) strategy was implemented. Layout features were quantified across four dimensions: coverage, connectivity, complexity, and aggregation. Key findings indicate:(1) After decoupling the background thermal effects of geographic location, green space and agricultural land are identified as the optimal land types for heat mitigation, while industrial land is the primary contributor to UHI intensification. In terms of land layout, coverage and connectivity exert significantly greater influence on the thermal environment than aggregation and complexity. (2) Residential and green space coverage exhibit monotonic associations with the UHI effect. In contrast, agricultural and industrial coverage demonstrate pronounced threshold effects, where their impacts stabilize after reaching specific levels.(3) The UHI attribution of land use displays significant spatial heterogeneity, most prominently in green space coverage, whose cooling efficiency is notably attenuated in high-density built-up areas.(4) The impacts of different land-use combinations on the UHI effect vary significantly, with some combinations generating synergistic effects while others exhibit spatial substitution. By identifying dominant land types and sensitive layout intervals, this study deepens the understanding of urban climate mechanisms and provides a scientific basis for formulating precise thermal environment management strategies.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107472.title: Unraveling the coupling-driven patterns of urban carbon emissions and urban heat islands: An LCZ-based interpretable machine learning approach
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107472.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107472.abstract: The coupling of Urban Carbon Emissions (UCE) and Urban Heat Islands (UHI) poses a critical challenge to sustainable urban development. While their static correlation is widely recognized, the mechanisms underlying their dynamic synchrony remain poorly understood. Furthermore, traditional urban morphological indicators are often limited in identifying priority intervention areas and may fail to capture the heterogeneity driven by diverse climatic and economic backgrounds. To address this, this study adopted the Local Climate Zone (LCZ) framework as a standardized physical descriptor to unravel UCE–UHI coupling patterns. Based on data from 2714 counties in China, we developed an XGBoost-TPE model combined with SHAP to facilitate mechanistic insights. Our key findings were as follows: (1) UCE and UHI in Chinese counties from 2015 to 2021 exhibited a significant global positive correlation (Moran’s I: 0.203–0.212, p-value < 0.01), but showed asynchronous dynamic changes in the northwest and western regions. (2) The LCZ-based model demonstrated high predictive consistency across all clusters (R2 of cross-validation > 0.85). (3) The key drivers of UCE and UHI exhibited heterogeneity: built-type LCZs appeared to be more critical for UCE, while natural-type LCZs tended to exert a more pronounced influence on UHI. (4) LCZs’ effects varied significantly with climatic backgrounds, with different directions, magnitudes, and transition thresholds (LCZs 2–3: 0.2%–6.9%, LCZs 4–6: 1.3%–20.5%, LCZs 7–10: 0.8%–13.9%, LCZs E-F: 1.2%–1.3%). (5) Synergistic, antagonistic, and complex phase-based compound interactions between LCZs were identified. By linking urban morphological characteristics with environmental responses, this study highlights the analytical potential of the LCZ framework for diagnosing UCE–UHI coupling dynamics. The results provide a quantitative, evidence-informed basis to support context-sensitive urban planning and targeted mitigation strategies.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107499.title: Nonlinear and spatially heterogeneous effects of the built environment on urban flood resilience: An interpretable spatially weighted machine learning framework
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107499.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107499.abstract: Urban flood disasters pose serious challenges to sustainable development and urban system functioning under climate change. Understanding the spatiotemporal patterns and mechanisms of urban flood resilience is therefore essential. To address model interpretability and spatial heterogeneity, this study develops an integrated analytical framework that incorporates dynamic assessment across the full resilience chain. Flood resilience is evaluated by combining the entropy weight method with a BP neural network to construct a three-dimensional system including robustness, resistance, and recovery. An interpretable geographically weighted machine learning model, GW-XGBoost-SHAP, is further developed to identify the nonlinear and spatially heterogeneous effects of built environment factors. The framework is applied to Guangzhou, China. Results show that flood resilience maintained a relatively stable spatial pattern from 2012 to 2022, with a dual-peak concentration in the central urban area and northern mountainous regions. Overall resilience increased from 0.131 to 0.179, while recovery showed the largest increase, from 0.366 to 0.433, highlighting the role of socioeconomic development in strengthening resilience. The GW-XGBoost-SHAP model outperformed comparable models, demonstrating the advantages of integrating geographically weighted mechanisms with machine learning. The effects of influencing factors varied across time and space, but land development intensity, land use diversity, emergency sheltering capacity, and social vulnerability remained key drivers. These factors showed clear nonlinear threshold effects and spatial heterogeneity. This study develops a quantitative framework for assessing dynamic flood resilience and its spatial drivers. The findings support land use planning, service facility allocation, landscape pattern optimization, and differentiated resilience improvement across zones, thereby informing climate adaptive urban flood management.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107508.title: Unraveling the impacts of multidimensional urban influencing factors on daytime and nighttime thermal environments across urban functional zones using SDGSAT-1 data and XGBoost-GeoShapley analysis
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107508.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107508.abstract: Although numerous researches have explored how urban influencing factors influences land surface temperature (LST), comparatively limited attention has been given to analyses based on urban functional zones (UFZs), especially those that investigate and contrast the driving mechanisms between daytime and nighttime conditions. Furthermore, numerous studies have analyzed this driving mechanism using interpretable machine learning methods that typically rely on the standard SHAP framework, yet this approach overlooks the inherent spatial dependency. In our study, high-resolution daytime and nighttime thermal infrared data from SDGSAT-1 were integrated with multi-source urban datasets for Fuzhou, China. An interpretable integrated XGBoost-GeoShapley framework was applied to comprehensively investigate the determinants of LST during summer daytime and nighttime among six predominant UFZs. The results reveal a fundamental daytime and nighttime shift in thermal drivers: built-environment indices dictate daytime sensible heat accumulation, whereas ecological factors dominate nocturnal latent heat cooling. Simultaneously building density acts as a severe daytime warmer but transitions to a relative nocturnal cooler in dense commercial cores due to the urban canyon mutual shading effect. Furthermore, ecological cooling demonstrates a biological threshold. Crucially, GeoShapley analysis uncovers that spatial interaction effects are substantially stronger at night, accounting for 38.2% of the integrated zone, with residential zones reaching 33.6%. This research establishes a spatially explicit analytical framework to unravel the multifactorial influences shaping the urban thermal environment and delivers scientific evidence that supports the development of spatially and temporally adaptive strategies for urban heat mitigation and planning.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107530.title: Artificial intelligence-related technologies for municipal solid waste management: A review and new insights from smart cities
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107530.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107530.abstract: Rapid urbanization, with over 55% of the global population in cities, has intensified challenges in municipal solid waste (MSW) management. Despite AI’s potential to optimize MSW systems, its applications remain underexplored. This study employs Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) topic modeling to analyze AI-driven MSW research and its evolution before and after COVID-19. Results show AI significantly enhances waste collection, sorting, and recycling efficiency, and identifies emerging research trends aligned with smart city needs. Based on these insights, we propose a three-stage AI-integrated framework, spanning IoT to Machine Learning, for Industry 4.0 to guide sustainable and resilient MSW management. The study highlights AI’s transformative role in enabling intelligent, data-driven, and sustainable urban waste governance.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107510.title: Deciphering the impacts of urban gray–green spaces on seasonal diurnal land surface temperature in a valley-basin city via explainable machine learning
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107510.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107510.abstract: The Urban Heat Island effect poses a major challenge to sustainable development, and understanding its driving factors is crucial for improving the urban thermal environment. The nonlinear effects of urban gray–green spaces on Land Surface Temperature (LST) under valley-basin conditions remain systematically underexplored. This study investigates Changsha, a typical valley-basin city, by integrating Morphological Spatial Pattern Analysis with landscape metrics to construct a comprehensive gray–green spaces framework. Using explainable machine learning (CatBoost-SHAP), we quantify the nonlinear and interactive effects of eight composite indicators on seasonal diurnal LST. Results show: (1) Gray space indicators contribute 51.6–59.2% to daytime LST across spring, summer, and winter, with BMSF as the dominant positive driver; green space indicators contribute 57.5–65.2% to nighttime LST, led by GACI and GMSF. (2) Threshold effects are evident: BMSF warming saturates beyond +0.5 SD, while GCI cooling diminishes after +0.5 SD, with marginal returns dropping from 0.25 °C per unit to near zero. GACI shows a unique positive effect (+0.3 °C) on winter nights. (3) Interactions reveal synergistic heating (BMSF×BCI > 0.25 SHAP), synergistic cooling (GMSF×GCI <−0.4 SHAP), and asymmetric buffering where high GMSF reduces BMSF thermal load by up to 0.6 SHAP. This study underscores gray–green interplay as a key driver of urban thermal dynamics in valley-basin cities, revealing quantifiable nonlinear balances. Based on these findings, we propose a regulatory strategy integrating spatiotemporal control, synergistic optimization, and topographic adaptation.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107513.title: Enhancing thermal resilience of heat–cold island networks in lake-ring urban agglomerations using machine learning and multi-scenario simulations
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107513.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107513.abstract: Under rapid urbanization and climate warming, urban heat island (UHI) effects in lake-ring urban agglomerations have intensified. Prior studies often emphasize single patches or local scales, obscuring regional heat–cold connectivity and limiting network-based resilience planning under future scenarios. This study integrates morphological spatial pattern analysis (MSPA) with circuit theory to construct a heat–cold island (HCI) composite network comprising sources, corridors, and nodes. In this framework, machine learning characterizes nonlinear thermal-connectivity resistance, while the patch-generating land-use simulation (PLUS) model simulates HCI network reorganization under multiple 2030 scenarios. A land surface temperature (LST)-derived surface thermal structural resilience framework was then developed to link historical and future network changes. Evidence from the Taihu Lake urban agglomeration indicates that from 2000 to 2020, heat island (HI) sources expanded rapidly across the eastern lakeside built-up area, with marked increases in corridors and nodes. In contrast, cold island (CI) networks became increasingly fragmented. HCI composite nodes shifted from the Taihu Lake shoreline toward the western ecological transition zone. By 2030, SSP585 formed a strong heat-connectivity network, and cooling connectivity pathways were nearly lost. Under SSP119, barriers to cold-source connectivity were reduced, and CI corridors increased. The surface thermal structural resilience improvement index (TR) showed strong structural dependence, remaining negative historically and declining further under SSP245 and SSP585. By contrast, SSP119 increased TR to −0.134 through cooling-corridor recovery and key-node reorganization, approaching a more balanced network structure. This study reframes LST-based surface thermal structural resilience from a whole-network HCI perspective and provides guidance for climate-adaptive spatial planning.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107557.title: Energy-logistics mutual feedback driven multi-agent dynamic interactive game model for low-carbon ports: Towards synergistic improvement of energy utilization and logistics management efficiency
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107557.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107557.abstract: The integration of offshore wind and tidal energy accelerates the green transition of port integrated energy systems (IES). However, collaborative energy optimization across the port and its surrounding residential, commercial, and industrial zones remains underexplored. To enhance energy utilization efficiency, a multi-agent dynamic interactive game model based on energy preference-oriented factors is proposed to resolve the interest conflicts between game agents in different regions. First, an energy-logistics mutual feedback strategy is developed, which introduces electric vehicles and hydrogen vehicles as new logistics equipment. This strategy enables the port logistics system to provide reverse power supply to the IES, thereby effectively improving energy utilization efficiency. Subsequently, a marginal benefit-based post-combustion carbon capture and storage (PCCS) scheduling strategy is introduced. By incorporating the PCCS, renewable energy utilization efficiency is further enhanced. Finally, a two-stage multi-agent dynamic interactive solving method is designed to derive an optimal energy dispatch scheme that simultaneously considers economic performance, environmental benefits, and robustness. Validated by the actual data from Tianjin Port, the proposed model reduces the overall economic cost and carbon emissions of the port-centric region by 1.57 % and 23.08 %, respectively. This study provides a novel framework and decision support for the low-carbon transition of multi-agent port regions.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107552.title: Attribution analysis of spatial mismatch between flood risk and public response: Insights from geospatial explainable artificial intelligence framework
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107552.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107552.abstract: During extreme urban flood events, the spatial mismatch between flood risk and public response can hinder timely flood management and equitable allocation of emergency resources. This research examines such mismatch at the community level during the “7.20 Extreme Rainfall” event in Zhengzhou, China, in 2021. We propose a geospatial explainable artificial intelligence (GeoXAI) framework to analyze the nonlinear and spatial non-stationary effects of influencing factors on this spatial mismatch. The framework enhances the spatial interpretability of model outcomes by integrating geospatial machine learning (ML) with GeoShapley. In this study, flood risk is defined as the probability of flood occurrence under given environmental conditions, rather than the depth or extent of flooding. Key findings include: (a) A significant spatial mismatch between flood risk and public response was identified within the study area. The central region is characterized by disproportionately high flood risk, whereas the western and southern regions exhibit disproportionately high public response; (b) Population density, night light index, and building density are key factors to the spatial mismatch, exhibiting strong nonlinear effects; (c) Population density dominates in central communities, while POI density most strongly affects peripheral communities in the southwest and northern regions; (d) The community location not only directly influences this spatial mismatch, but also plays a role through spatial interactions with other factors. This research enhances the comprehension of the spatial mismatch between flood risk and public response, highlighting its implications for improving governmental flood response and flood preparedness at community and individual levels.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107539.title: Learning from residuals: a knowledge-data-driven hybrid model for explaining the social-ecological influences on urban agglomeration resilience
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107539.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107539.abstract: The sustainable development of urban agglomerations is increasingly threatened by the social and ecological pressures, and deserves an in-depth understanding for resilience enhancement. However, the classic knowledge-driven models, which pre-define linear relationships and influencing pathways, fail to fully capture these complicated effects, resulting in high residuals. To address this, we propose a knowledge-data-driven hybrid model that uses residuals to bridge the two models. This framework integrates XGBoost-SHAP with partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) to quantify the spatial bias of social-ecological influences on resilience from a pressure-state-response perspective. The proposed model was applied to 271 counties in the Central Plains Urban Agglomeration (CPUA) from 2010 to 2020, an area covering 30 cities across five provinces. The main findings include: 1) The proposed hybrid model attained the highest R² value and the lowest RMSE value, demonstrating excellent overall fit and prediction accuracy of urban agglomeration resilience. 2) The influence of social factors on resilience exhibits a significant threshold effect, whereby the negative impact of social pressure becomes underestimated once the threshold is exceeded.
