Meanwhile, social response follows an inverted U-shaped pattern, suggesting that investigation within the optimal policy window can maximize the resilience. 3) Ecological impacts show directional gradients, with north-south pressure and east-west state gradients being prominent. The south is facing the urgency of alleviating ecological pressure, while the positive effect of ecosystem service value in the west remains insufficiently valued. 4) Linear models overestimate the importance of responses and underestimate the destructive impact of pressure. Therefore, resources should be shifted from response-oriented intervention measures to stress mitigation measures. Moreover, dynamic monitoring of social and ecological states is needed to prevent deterioration from having a negative impact on resilience. These findings provide practical implications for urban policing strategies aimed at enhancing the urban agglomeration resilience.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107573.title: Precision governance for urban decarbonization: Decoupling passenger and freight transport emissions by integrating explainable AI and clustering
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107573.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107573.abstract: Developing low-carbon urban transportation systems is critical for achieving Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) 11 and 13. A fundamental obstacle to effective decarbonization is the persistent reliance on one-size-fits-all policies that conflate the distinct emission pathways of passenger and freight road transport. To address this gap, we propose a targeted governance paradigm and develop an integrated explainable AI-spatial clustering framework to decouple and diagnose the heterogeneous emission-socioeconomic associations of the two sectors. Applied to high-resolution vehicle trajectory data from Guangzhou, a global laboratory for rapid urbanization, our framework delineates four spatially distinct clusters based on shared emission-driver profiles. Results reveal a fundamental spatial and functional divergence: passenger emissions concentrate in the urban core and correlate positively with population density and commercial land use, while freight emissions exhibit a broader peri‑urban distribution with an inverse relationship to population density. Crucially, we identify nonlinear threshold effects for key predictors and demonstrate that the same factor (e.g., distance to the CBD) can exert opposite directional effects on the two sectors across different zones. Based on these findings, we develop a dual-track decarbonization strategy that differentiates interventions between passenger-dominant and freight-dominant clusters, providing empirically validated, threshold-based planning levers for targeted mitigation. This study demonstrates that spatially differentiated, data-driven governance is essential for maximizing decarbonization efficacy under resource constraints. The proposed modular framework is transferable to other megacities worldwide, offering a replicable tool for advancing low-carbon urban transportation.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107585.title: Identifying CO2 emission reduction strategies tailored to different building types by integrating multi-scale factors via deep learning
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107585.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107585.abstract: Reducing carbon emissions in the building sector is a critical challenge for urban decarbonization. Buildings differ substantially in their functions, usage intensities, and operational characteristics, which require emission reduction strategies tailored to different building types. However, previous studies have been limited in their examination of how building-level characteristics and the surrounding urban environments jointly influence CO2 emissions across different building types. Therefore, this study proposes an artificial intelligence-based analytical framework that integrates building-level characteristics with urban environmental factors to assess their effects on CO2 emissions across different building types. This framework captures non-linear relationships between the multi-scale factors and CO2 emissions and assesses their effects using model interpretation techniques, simulating changes from current states. The findings of this study indicate that increasing floor area ratio (FAR) generally reduces CO2 emissions, whereas emissions increase in public buildings when the FAR is increased by 140% relative to its current level. Increasing south-facing building surface area showed the potential to substantially reduce emissions in low-rise residential and public buildings. Furthermore, the increased green area ratio (GAR) effectively mitigated emissions in residential buildings, while exhibiting a rebound effect in commercial buildings when increased by 12%. These findings highlight the importance of building-type-specific and threshold-based strategies for effective urban building decarbonization. Moreover, this framework provides quantitative evidence for developing building-type-specific regulatory standards and design guidelines, supporting more targeted and effective urban building decarbonization.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107556.title: A hybrid MCDM integrating XGBoost and explainable AI to assess urban ecosystem resilience and identify contributors: A case of Chinese cities
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107556.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107556.abstract: Urban ecosystem resilience (ER) is a fundamental prerequisite for global sustainable development in the face of accelerating urbanization and climate instability. Conventional frameworks, however, predominantly rely on linear aggregation schemes and provide limited interpretability regarding the relative contributions of different indicators. Here we present a hybrid framework integrating multi-criteria decision-making (MCDM) with explainable artificial intelligence (AI) to evaluate resilience and examine feature attribution patterns. By applying this approach to 292 Chinese cities from 2010 to 2022, we constructed a composite resilience index encompassing resistance, recovery, adaptability, and transformability. We show that national resilience increased by 28.69% over the study period, with adaptability emerging as the dominant dimension. The SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analysis is used to characterize feature attribution patterns within the model. Feature contributions vary across their value ranges, reflecting heterogeneity in model-attributed contributions under the joint distribution of features (e.g., the contribution of urban green space is higher within certain value intervals and relatively smaller outside these ranges). These findings provide a transparent, data-driven pathway for quantifying complex urban dynamics, offering actionable insights for policymakers to optimize resilience strategies under uncertainty.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107608.title: Enhancing interdependent infrastructure systems resilience in post-disaster recovery: A social-technical approach based on reinforcement learning
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107608.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107608.abstract: A social-technical approach integrating the Infrastructure Hetero-functional Graph (IHFG) and Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) is proposed for the collaborative recovery of post-disaster multi-infrastructure systems. A "physical entity–functional node–service process" mapping mechanism is established to explicitly characterize complex system interdependencies. Furthermore, a reward mechanism driven by hierarchical resident needs is integrated to facilitate service-oriented recovery within highly dynamic and complex environments. In a case study of a coupled transportation-power-gas-water network in Jingdezhen, optimal repair strategies under multi-hazard scenarios were explored. The results show that IHFG-MARL with dynamic weights can generate system-level recovery strategies that account for complex interdependencies and achieve relatively robust resilience improvement under different disaster conditions. In rainfall-driven scenarios, the proposed method and the genetic algorithm both show strong performance, whereas the advantage of IHFG-MARL with dynamic weights becomes more evident under the full-damage stress-test scenario. This indicates that the proposed method has stronger strategic adaptability in complex interdependent networks and under high-intensity disturbances. In addition, the embedded dynamic demand mechanism enables the recovery process to prioritize residents’ basic survival needs and gradually shift toward broader functional service needs as recovery progresses, thereby forming recovery pathways consistent with the hierarchical evolution of residents’ needs.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107586.title: A comparative assessment of sampling strategies for tree-based machine learning models in urban flood susceptibility prediction with imbalanced data
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107586.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107586.abstract: Flood susceptibility mapping identifies flood-prone areas, providing scientific support for flood prevention planning and resilient infrastructure. However, the accuracy of machine learning models in flood susceptibility mapping is compromised by imbalanced data. Moreover, systematic comparative assessments of sampling strategies for tree-based models in urban flood susceptibility prediction are lacking, and the intricate nonlinear correlations between flood susceptibility and its underlying drivers remain insufficiently explored. This study developed a novel framework that systematically investigates the effect of sampling methods and non-flooding samples ratios on tree-based models (Random Forest, XGBoost, and LightGBM) in urban flood susceptibility prediction in Beijing, China, and places a dual emphasis on predictive performance and model interpretability via Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) and Partial Dependence Plot (PDP) analyses to interpret the key drivers. Results show that models using one-class support vector machine (OC SVM) method (Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC) ≥ 0.92) consistently outperformed those using random sampling at 1:3 and 1:5 ratios. Specifically, Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM) model with OC SVM at a 1:3 ratio attained the highest AUC value (0.938) and Geometric Mean (G-mean) (0.845) across all sampling methods and ratios, and exhibited a more balanced and rational spatial pattern in flood susceptibility prediction. The top four factors contributing to flood susceptibility were Gross Domestic Product (GDP) level (28.04%), mean building height (15.96%), distance to roads (15.31%), and Digital Elevation Model (DEM) (9.67%). PDP analysis revealed urban flood susceptibility initially increases significantly with GDP, and then declines and stabilizes after a critical point. A strong near-linear positive relationship was evident between building height and flood susceptibility. Flood susceptibility significantly decreases as distance to roads increased and eventually stabilizes. This study provides empirical evidence and methodological guidance for selecting sampling strategies in applying machine learning models for urban flood susceptibility prediction.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107589.title: Automated urban energy assessment: From thermal flyover to AI-driven retrofit prioritization for sustainable cities
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107589.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107589.abstract: Cities urgently need scalable methods to assess building energy performance for retrofit prioritization, yet current approaches are costly and slow for comprehensive urban energy planning. We present an automated pipeline that transforms thermal flyovers into actionable energy assessments using AI-driven analysis. Our approach segments mid-wave infrared orthomosaics into building patches using an unsupervised multi-modal pipeline (Thermal-SAM), extracts physically interpretable ring and context features, and benchmarks energy-use intensity (EUI) derived from aggregated EPC records. We exclude implausible EUI records above 1000 kWh/m2/yr from primary model-performance evaluation. On this screened dataset (n=1190), leakage-free non-thermal covariates achieve RMSE = 26.84 and MAE = 16.13 kWh/m2/yr, within the range reported by recent EPC-based prediction studies. An EPC-full upper-bound model that retains energy-consumption proxies achieves lower error (RMSE = 9.36, MAE = 1.31 kWh/m2/yr), but this reflects feature–target proximity rather than independent prediction. Thermal features are therefore not presented as routine direct EUI predictors. Instead, the excluded high-EUI tail is treated as a diagnostic anomaly set: in the unfiltered diagnostic analysis, thermal features help rank the largest thermal–EPC discrepancies (AUC = 0.779, 95% CI 0.774–0.784, 100 seeds), while this signal collapses after the implausible records are removed. These findings reposition thermal flyovers as a scalable tool for triaging buildings with unusually high or inconsistent EPC-derived energy use, while highlighting the limitations of single-pass thermal data for accurate EUI regression. Reproducible code (available upon request) supports rapid, citywide screening and targeted follow-up audits.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107687.title: Urban morphology as a driver of urban sustainability trade-offs and synergies: an explainable graph neural network analysis of Singapore
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107687.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107687.abstract:
Abstract
Urban development in high-density cities must balance economic growth, environmental performance, and social well-being, yet how urban form mediates the coupling between these dimensions remains poorly quantified and seldom interpretable. This study introduces a data-driven framework for diagnosing and optimizing the environmental and socio-economic performance of dense urban environments. We adopt the CRITIC-Entropy method to construct two composite metrics—the Environmental Cost and Stress Index (ECSI) and the Socio-Economic Vitality Index (SEVI)—and apply them to Singapore as a high-density urban testbed. Using 15 key urban morphological parameters, we train a Graph Neural Network (GNN) and employ explainable AI (XAI), specifically GNNExplainer coupled with Partial Dependence Plots (PDP), to uncover the non-linear and spatially embedded relationships between urban morphology and these (eco-socio-economic) performance outcomes. The framework identifies four Pareto-frontier archetypes that characterize distinct morphology–performance pathways. Distance to the central business district, building coverage ratio, and greenery coverage ratio are the most dominant drivers of environmental cost, while building-height diversity, land-cover diversity, and sky view factor most strongly shape socio-economic vitality. Across the 15 indicators, most relationships are synergistic or mixed, with genuine trade-offs concentrated in a small set of dominant drivers, notably building coverage ratio and distance to the central business district. Central districts generally exhibit the strongest spillover benefits for both dimensions (ECSI and SEVI) relative to peripheral areas. These results provide interpretable and actionable benchmarks for site-specific retrofitting and targeted urban regeneration in high-density cities.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107619.title: Revealing the diurnal drivers of land surface temperature using artificial neural network models: A case study in Changsha-Zhuzhou-Xiangtan metropolitan area, China
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107619.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107619.abstract: Rapid urbanization has intensified the urban heat island (UHI) effect, highlighting the need to better understand the factors associated with land surface temperature (LST) in order to improve local thermal environments. Although previous studies have shown that urbanization and environmental conditions can significantly influence LST, their relative importance, nonlinear relationships, and differences between daytime and nighttime remain insufficiently understood. The Changsha-Zhuzhou-Xiangtan (CZT) metropolitan area, one of China’s first national pilot zones for building a resource-efficient and environment-friendly society, is a representative metropolitan region characterized by a compact polycentric structure and pronounced natural-urban spatial heterogeneity. Using artificial neural network models and Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP), this study identifies the relative importance and nonlinear associations of multiple spatial and environmental factors with daytime and nighttime LST. This analysis is data-driven, and the physical mechanisms discussed in this study are intended only as plausible interpretations of the observed patterns rather than as directly tested processes. The results show that: (1) Elevation had the strongest association with both daytime and nighttime LST, followed by indicators of human activity intensity; (2) water bodies and densely vegetated areas exhibited clear cooling effects during the daytime, whereas water bodies showed relatively higher LST at night, shifting from daytime cold spots to nighttime hot spots; (3) all factors exhibited nonlinear associations with LST, and marginal effect curves revealed critical ranges and inflection points for daytime and nighttime LST variations; and (4) nonlinear statistical approaches are useful for quantitatively characterizing the complex relationships between LST and multiple spatial-environmental factors at the metropolitan scale. These findings provide refined and differentiated decision support for urban heat mitigation and spatial planning.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107629.title: Prioritizing ‘greenable areas’ for urban heat relief by integrating heat risk, cooling potential, and welfare equity: A data-driven framework with a case study of Nanjing, China
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107629.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107629.abstract: Urban heat risk is intensifying in compact, high-density cities where opportunities for new green space are limited. Existing prioritization studies often identify where cooling is needed, but less often ask whether greening is feasible or where it would yield the largest marginal benefit. This study introduces greenable areas, defined as residual urban spaces that can be converted to vegetation within dense built-up fabrics. We develop a decision-support workflow that identifies these spaces, assesses heat risk, predicts scenario-based LST cooling with a machine-learning model, and estimates welfare gains in population-weighted green-space accessibility, with all outputs aggregated to street blocks. A case study in the main urban area of Nanjing, China shows how the framework can produce priority maps for feasible infill greening under limited land resources. By linking need, feasibility, cooling potential, and welfare equity, the study provides a replicable screening approach for urban heat adaptation in space-constrained environments.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107688.title: Strategic and equitable allocation of electric vehicle fast charging stations using geospatial-aware multi-objective deep reinforcement learning
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107688.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107688.abstract: Public fast charging infrastructure is becoming an essential component of sustainable urban mobility as cities transition toward low-carbon transportation (e.g., Electric Vehicles (EVs)). However, suboptimal deployment can exacerbate spatial disparities in service accessibility, limit the practical benefits of EV adoption, and create localized stress on urban distribution grids. Despite recent advances in the allocation and placement of electric vehicle fast charging stations (FCSs), existing decision-support approaches remain limited in their ability to coordinate multiple objectives across large, spatially heterogeneous urban systems. This study thus proposes a multi-objective sequential decision-making model for the placement and sizing of FCS, integrated with solar power supply, across large and complex urban environments. By integrating a federated learning-based multi-objective deep reinforcement learning (FLMODRL) framework with geospatial analysis, the proposed model identifies EVFCS sites through a global policy that aggregates locally learned policies to achieve balanced performance across environmental, economic, and urbanity objectives. The proposed FLMORL model shows it capability to determine both the optimal placement and capacity of FCS by outperforming single-agent weight-summed reward scalarization deep reinforcement learning (DRL). Specifically, the model identifies 520 fast charging stations in Chicago that exceed a high reward threshold (e.g., >10), indicating locations that simultaneously satisfy all objectives. In addition, the proposed deployment scenario suggests the potential of the learned spatial allocation strategy to improve population-weighted accessibility across income groups in Chicago. Overall, the results demonstrate the model’s effectiveness in supporting strategic and accessibility-aware FCS allocation across the urban area, contributing to more sustainable and resilient charging infrastructure planning.
keywords: Allocation and placement of charging stations

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107711.title: Assessing urban waterlogging risk and nonlinear drivers in high density cities: A multi model machine learning comparative approach
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107711.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107711.abstract: Under the combined pressures of climate change and rapid urbanization, high density cities are facing increasing risks of urban waterlogging (UW) during extreme rainfall events. However, existing UW risk assessments often lack systematic comparisons of different machine learning models and provide limited insight into nonlinear driving mechanisms. Taking Shenzhen, a representative high density city in China, as a case study, this research develops an integrated assessment framework that combines multi source spatial data, multi model machine learning comparison, and explainable artificial intelligence techniques. Thirteen risk factors are selected from the perspectives of hazard, environmental susceptibility, and exposure. Four ensemble tree-based models, namely Random Forest, Gradient Boosting Decision Tree, Extreme Gradient Boosting, and Light Gradient Boosting Machine, are applied and compared for UW risk prediction. The results show that the RF model achieves the best overall performance, with high-risk areas identified by the model covering 92.45% of historical UW locations. Spatially, UW risk in Shenzhen exhibits a pronounced southeast low and northwest high pattern, closely associated with highly urbanized and densely populated areas. Model SHAP and PDP analyses further reveal strong nonlinear and threshold effects among key risk factors. Impervious surface area, population density, and GDP are identified as the most influential factors associated with UW risk. In particular, road density shows a pronounced U-shaped relationship with UW risk, highlighting the dual role of road systems in drainage organization and impervious surface expansion. Overall, this study provides a transferable framework for resilience governance and spatial optimization in high density cities.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107704.title: Nonlinear driving mechanisms of land surface temperature under the coupling of blue-green space and urbanization: An analysis based on explainable machine learning
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107704.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107704.abstract: Urban thermal stress has intensified under climate change and rapid urbanization. Blue-green space (BGS) is a key form of ecological infrastructure for mitigating urban heat; however, its thermal effects are jointly shaped by landscape patterns, urbanization intensity, and development-stage differences. Using Zhengzhou, China, as a case study, this study integrated blue-green space–urbanization coupling with interpretable land surface temperature (LST) modelling by combining coupling coordination degree (CCD) classification, Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) attribution, robustness tests, and breakpoint validation. The results showed that CCD increased continuously from 2003 to 2023 and exhibited a clustered spatial pattern, with higher values in the urban core and lower values in the suburban fringe. The dominant drivers of LST varied across CCD gradients. In the low-coordination gradient, the primary model-attributed driver shifted from built-up percentage (BP) to forest percentage (FP), whereas in the middle- and higher-coordination gradients, water percentage (WP) and population density (POP) generally showed stronger contributions to model predictions. Nonlinear response analysis indicated that the effects of key blue-green-space and urbanization indicators were stage-dependent rather than governed by fixed thresholds. Fractional vegetation cover (FVC) exhibited the most consistent model-derived response interval, with nonlinear changes concentrated around 0.55–0.63 in the middle and later periods. BP showed later-stage warming-related warning intervals, mainly around 0.79–0.81, in middle- and higher-coordination gradients. WP showed weaker temporal stability, with a case-specific response interval around 0.17 observed mainly in the 2023 higher-coordination gradient. These findings provide case-based, model-derived evidence for differentiated heat-mitigation strategies in Zhengzhou and offer a methodological reference for testing similar coupled urban systems elsewhere.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107724.title: Where could urban tree canopy expansion lower modeled summer cooling-energy demand? An equity-informed explainable machine-learning framework for Washington, DC
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107724.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107724.abstract: Urban heat and rising summer cooling demand are increasingly important equity concerns in U.S. cities, yet fine-scale evidence on where urban greening may reduce summer cooling-energy demand remains limited. This study examines modeled summer cooling-energy demand across Census Block Groups (CBGs) in Washington, DC, with emphasis on the environmental and social conditions shaping neighborhood-scale cooling demand and the potential role of targeted tree-canopy expansion. We integrate indicators of tree canopy, imperviousness, planting opportunity, and neighborhood deprivation. Using spatially cross-validated XGBoost with a monotonic canopy constraint, SHAP-based interpretation, threshold identification, and counterfactual canopy scenarios, we identify where canopy intervention is most likely to provide benefit. Results show that modeled cooling demand is spatially concentrated in Wards 7 and 8, where higher deprivation, lower canopy, and less favorable built-environment conditions coincide. In contrast, Ward 3 exhibits the lowest deprivation, highest canopy, and lowest modeled cooling demand. Imperviousness alone does not fully explain modeled cooling demand: some areas show high imperviousness but relatively lower demand, suggesting that housing quality and broader socioeconomic advantage may condition the energy consequences of heat exposure. Areas with lower tree canopy tended to exhibit higher modeled cooling-energy demand, although this pattern varied with surrounding environmental and built-environment conditions. A model-derived canopy screening benchmark of approximately 21% in Wards 7 and 8 suggests that the strongest modeled cooling benefits are likely to occur in low-canopy neighborhoods below this benchmark. In both wards, about 64% of CBGs fell below the threshold. Planting opportunity emerges as the strongest implementation-relevant predictor. Overall, the findings provide an equity-centered framework for targeting urban greening to reduce modeled cooling-energy demand and support climate adaptation.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107749.title: SHAP-TAG: Operationalizing explainable AI for urban heat governance through attribution-severity typologies and policy triggers
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107749.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107749.abstract: Urban heat adaptation increasingly relies on spatially explicit diagnostics, yet explainable AI outputs often remain difficult to translate into planning decisions. This study introduces SHAP-TAG (SHAP-based Typology and Actionable Governance), a framework that converts grid-level SHAP attributions into governance-ready products: attribution-severity typologies, model-based transition zones, and a tiered policy matrix. Using 30-m summer daytime land surface temperature (LST) modeling for the Greater Taipei Metropolitan Area, we distinguish a global diagnostic model from an urban action model to reduce topographic masking and focus interpretation on governance-facing built-environment drivers. The urban action model achieved a spatial cross-validation R² of 0.540 and MAE of 1.85°C using nine actionable variables. Compared with the global diagnostic model, NDVI became the dominant governance-facing signal in the urban action model, rising from rank 4 to rank 1 and showing a 2.31-fold increase in mean absolute SHAP magnitude. Full-urban SHAP clustering identified four attribution-severity tiers structured primarily by a vegetation-deficit and built-up-intensity gradient, with secondary modulation from openness and surface-composition signals: Strong vegetation–openness cooling core (10.73%), Moderate vegetation-cooling context (18.53%), Near-neutral transitional zone (33.35%), and Vegetation-deficit warming-priority zone (37.39%). These tiers are interpreted as a SHAP-calibrated governance sequence rather than four mutually independent heat mechanisms. NDVI showed a primary SHAP sign-change around 0.275 (95% bootstrap CI: 0.273–0.277), with the operational transition zone spanning approximately 0.27–0.33 when combined with sensitivity-based references. Albedo and sky-view-related indicators exhibited context-dependent attribution patterns and were therefore treated as operational references rather than universal physical thresholds. By linking attribution direction and magnitude, transition zones, and policy tiers, SHAP-TAG provides a locally calibrated but workflow-transferable approach for urban heat governance.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107720.title: Predicting citywide human mobility with a graph-prior-enhanced euclidean convolutional network
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107720.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107720.abstract: Fine-grained human mobility prediction at the urban scale is crucial for urban traffic management and sustainable development. However, existing models struggle to balance prediction accuracy and computational efficiency in urban-scale, fine-grained scenarios: models based on Euclidean structure suffer from limited accuracy, while models based on non-Euclidean structure face prohibitive computational costs. To address this challenge, we propose a Graph-Prior-Enhanced Euclidean Convolutional Network (GPECN) for efficient and accurate citywide mobility prediction. First, inspired by structural similarity, we present a virtual graph based on Wasserstein distance to capture the irregular and heterogeneous spatial relationships among OD pairs. Second, we embed graph priors into a Euclidean grid, forming a graph-prior-enhanced structure that preserves the accuracy advantages of graph models while retaining the computational efficiency of grid-based models. Finally, we explicitly incorporate the graph priors into the forward propagation of a classical convolutional neural network, enabling effective emulation of urban-scale graph feature aggregation under a low computational load. Using real world OD flow data from Xiamen and Fuzhou, China, we demonstrated the effectiveness of the proposed model at the urban scale. Experimental results show that, compared with five baseline models, the proposed GPECN model achieves prediction accuracy on a par with that of graph models while significantly improving computational efficiency.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107799.title: Exploring the impacts of logistics space on urban carbon emissions: A hybrid MNL-LightGBM method
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107799.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107799.abstract: As a major source of urban carbon emissions, logistics space and its interaction with the surrounding environment have become critical to understanding the dynamic patterns of urban carbon emissions. Deeper investigation into how urban logistics land use and facility layouts contribute to the spatial heterogeneity of carbon emissions holds significant implications. Taking the Wuhan Metropolitan Development Area as a case study, this paper proposes the concept of Spatial Environment Induced Carbon-Emission Discrepancy (SEICD), which quantifies emission heterogeneity into carbon mitigation and carbon exacerbation. A hybrid MNL‑LightGBM model is constructed to identify key factors and reveal their nonlinear mechanisms, focusing on the combined effects of logistics facility layout and spatial variables on carbon emissions. Results show that spatial variables, such as industrial land proportion and floor area ratio, exhibit strong nonlinear associations with SEICD. Interactive associations between the number of logistics facilities and distance to small facilities, as well as with FAR and distance to residential land, play particularly prominent roles. Furthermore, grid-scale analysis based on the SHAP method reveals that the layout of large logistics facilities adjacent to industrial land in the urban periphery, as well as areas with high floor area ratio and high land use mix in the central urban area, are conducive to carbon mitigation. By integrating mechanisms across different functional zones, this study constructs an optimization framework and regulatory methods for logistics facility layout based on spatial environmental adaptability, providing quantitative support and planning guidance for the low‑carbon transition of urban logistics systems.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107776.title: Revealing associations between urban infrastructure and U5MR in sub-Saharan Africa through interpretable machine learning
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107776.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107776.abstract: Rapid urbanization is reshaping child survival in sub-Saharan Africa (SSA), yet associations between urban infrastructure and under-five mortality (U5MR) have been examined nationally or through an urban-rural lens, leaving nonlinearity and development-stage heterogeneity poorly characterized. The classical Preston curve describes a log-linear relationship between economic development and health, but its applicability across African cities with uneven infrastructure remains unresolved. We integrated OpenStreetMap, remote sensing, and gridded socioeconomic data for 905 functional urban areas in 36 countries from a 40-country source frame and used CatBoost with SHAP to characterize nonlinear associations between 14 city-level indicators and U5MR. Our study can be summarized in three parts: (1) Under country-stratified five-fold cross-validation, CatBoost explained 70.4% of the variance in log U5MR, while OSM-completeness, household-survey, PM₂.₅, and spatial analyses defined interpretation limits. (2) SHAP analyses showed that the Preston relationship did not hold uniformly at the city scale. GDP per capita shifted from positive model contributions in low- and middle-GDP cities to negative contributions in high-GDP cities. Electricity grid density showed negative contributions in middle- and high-GDP cities, whereas road density was negative only in the high-GDP group. (3) Pairwise interactions were feature dependent; interaction-to-main-effect ratios ranged from 63.9% to 174.9%, indicating that urban child health is better understood as a coupled system than as a target for any single intervention. These findings provide a city-level diagnostic framework for child health under the sustainable urbanization agenda and demonstrate interpretable machine learning’s potential for revealing urban-system complexity.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107766.title: Bus passenger flow prediction with a dynamic graph neural network and bidirectional gated recurrent unit
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107766.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107766.abstract: Short-term passenger flow prediction is critical for the real-time management of urban bus systems. Several unresolved challenges persist, including how to account for abrupt station or route silence, fluctuating accessibility due to variable speeds caused by traffic, and the dynamic evolution of spatial dependencies across the transit network. To address these challenges, we propose the Dynamic Graph Convolutional Network–Bidirectional Gated Recurrent Unit (DGCN-BiGRU) model. The model first constructs a dynamic graph by capturing real-world station and route changes, reflecting disruptions in daily operations. It then incorporates speed-adjusted accessibility matrices, which quantify travel ease between stops under varying traffic conditions. Through dynamic graph convolution, it learns evolving spatial dependencies between stations. To capture temporal patterns, a Bidirectional Gated Recurrent Unit (BiGRU) learns both forward and backward dependencies in time series data. In addition, the model introduces a multi-source temporal fusion framework that integrates recent historical, weather-aligned, and holiday-aligned data. To capture heterogeneous temporal dependencies from diverse passenger flow regimes, we design a multi-branch temporal encoding framework with adaptive fusion. Specifically, the pipeline comprises three stages: Feature Enhancement by Self-Attention, Stream-Wise Gating, and Adaptive Convolutional Fusion. These jointly allow the model to highlight salient temporal patterns from different branches while suppressing redundant or noisy signals, improving multi-step forecast stability and accuracy. Empirical evaluations on real-world public transit data from Ames, Iowa (featuring frequent station silence) demonstrate that DGCN-BiGRU outperforms state-of-the-art models in accuracy and robustness, particularly under high-fluctuation scenarios. The model further shows robustness to seasonal interference through cross-month validation and generalizability on the larger-scale EXO dataset, suggesting that DGCN-BiGRU offers a scalable and seasonally robust solution for real-time bus passenger flow forecasting.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107812.title: Data-driven eco-routing for optimizing energy efficient electric vehicle driving
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107812.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107812.abstract: Electric vehicle (EV) adoption is accelerating globally, yet limited driving range and sensitivity to operating conditions remain critical barriers to sustainable urban mobility. Existing navigation systems optimize for travel time or distance and rarely account for the joint effects of traffic, road grade, and wind on EV energy demand. This study develops a data-driven eco-routing framework that couples a physics-based EV energy consumption model with multi-source, network-scale data for the state of California. The energy model captures aerodynamic drag, rolling resistance, grade resistance, and regenerative braking at the link level, and uses wind-tunnel-based drag coefficients, a logarithmic wind profile for vehicle-height correction, and hourly traffic speeds from the Caltrans Performance Measurement System. The 243,072-link California road network is evaluated under three traffic and wind scenarios, together with a directional wind sensitivity analysis. Compared to distance- and time-optimal routing, eco-routing reduces trip energy consumption by up to 54% and 74%, respectively, on a representative Glendale–Rancho Cucamonga corridor. Wind direction alone changes cumulative route energy by up to 29% between headwind and tailwind conditions while route geometry, traffic, and terrain are held fixed. These results demonstrate that directional wind and terrain-aware eco-routing can meaningfully extend EV range, reduce charging demand, and support energy-efficient mobility planning in sustainable cities and regions.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107817.title: Urban shrinkage and carbon emission prediction structures: A methodological extension using interpretable machine learning
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107817.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107817.abstract: Against the background of slowing population growth, reuse of existing built-up space, and binding local fiscal constraints, urban low-carbon governance is shaped by low-growth conditions. Whether urban shrinkage is associated with lower carbon emissions remains insufficiently explained. Existing studies often identify shrinkage through negative population or economic growth, thereby capturing cities already experiencing visible decline but providing limited insight into low-growth cities whose growth remains positive yet decelerating. Using data for 108 cities in the Yangtze River Economic Belt from 2012 to 2022, this study constructs a multidimensional framework for identifying urban shrinkage across population, economic, social, and spatial structural dimensions, and applies XGBoost-SHAP to examine predictive associations, response boundaries, and non-additive combinations between shrinkage-related variables and carbon emissions. The results show that urban shrinkage in the region is characterized primarily by the diffusion of relative rather than absolute shrinkage. From 2017 to 2022, 59.26% of cities are classified as shrinking, 52.78% exhibit relative shrinkage, whereas only 6.48% exhibit absolute shrinkage. Shrinkage status does not mechanically correspond to declining emissions, average city-level emissions increase from 5.9209 to 9.0622 million tons, 84.4% of shrinking cities still record emission growth, and high-emission clusters remain embedded in metropolitan areas and the industrial corridor along the Yangtze River. Model interpretation indicates that shrinkage status is not associated with a uniform downward shift in response boundaries. Instead, population activity, consumption demand, transport services, built-up space, and ecological capacity enter the emission-prediction structure selectively. Conceptually, the study incorporates relative shrinkage as a pre-decline low-growth condition in carbon emissions analysis. Methodologically, it uses XGBoost-SHAP to characterize predictive response boundaries and non-additive configurations, shifting the interpretation from absolute decline and demand reduction toward relative shrinkage, flow–stock misalignment, and conditional predictive structures. The findings support stock renewal, infrastructure adaptation, governance of idle land, and regional coordination in low-growth cities.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107846.title: LLM-empowered agents for lifeline network recovery with graph-guided MCP tools
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107846.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107846.abstract: Post-disaster recovery of lifelines is critical, with numerous studies proposing tools for interdependent lifeline network recovery (LNR). However, existing tools themselves, whether standalone or embedded in systems, lack task-solving capabilities and still depend on human orchestration and execution for handling LNR tasks. Hence, this study proposes a development approach of large language model (LLM)-empowered agents that can intelligently utilize tools to solve LNR tasks. The approach comprises (i) the development of graph-guided LNR tools hosted on model context protocol (MCP) servers, (ii) the construction of LNR agents with the pattern of tool chain generation-tool execution (TCG-TE), and (iii) the evaluation and comparison of agents’ performance. The findings indicate that among the 32 compared agents, 5 out of 8 TCG-TE agents can successfully solve 50 LNR tasks, while none of the 24 traditional agents can solve all tasks. Agents following TCG-TE pattern with graph-guided MCP tools empowered by 8 LLMs solve 13.9% more tasks and reduce 68.2% of unnecessary tool invocations compared to the best-performing agents in traditional patterns. This study contributes by providing a development approach of LNR agents with task-solving capacities. Moreover, the proposed TCG-TE pattern alleviates agents’ difficulty in selecting and orchestrating tools.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107876.title: Environmental justice and urban heat thresholds in Istanbul: An explainable machine learning approach with spatial residual diagnostics
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107876.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107876.abstract: Rapid urbanization intensifies the Urban Heat Island (UHI) effect, yet neighborhood-level surface thermal exposure remains unevenly distributed across urban populations. While the environmental justice dimensions of UHI have received attention in Global North contexts, empirical evidence from rapidly developing megacities remains limited, and conventional machine learning applications in urban climatology frequently overlook spatial autocorrelation, risking biased inference. To address these gaps, this study develops a hybrid spatial machine learning framework to examine the drivers of mean summer Land Surface Temperature (LST)—a radiometric surface temperature proxy, not a direct measure of thermal comfort—across 750 neighborhoods in Istanbul. An XGBoost regressor was integrated with a post-hoc Spatial Error Model (SEM) diagnostic filter, reducing residual Moran's I from 0.449 (p = 0.001) to −0.011 (p = 0.321) under a district-grouped spatial cross-validation design (Test R² = 0.937; CV R² = 0.870 ± 0.070). SHAP analysis was applied to a 25-variable dataset fusing Landsat 8/9 remote sensing imagery, NASA SRTM topographic data, and neighborhood-level socioeconomic records to quantify non-linear feature contributions to LST. NDBI and NDVI emerged as the primary morphological determinants, followed by distance to coastline and population density. A density-dependent vegetation efficacy transition band was estimated at approximately 27,000–34,000 persons/km² (primary breakpoint estimate: 28,070; bootstrap 95% CI: 27,176–30,744; district-grouped spatial sensitivity range: 26,914–34,312 persons/km²), above which NDVI cooling contributions diminish substantially regardless of greenness level. A systematic thermal disparity was identified across socioeconomic groups: A+ (elite) neighborhoods exhibited a mean summer LST of 39.4 °C, compared with 42.8 °C in D (low SES) neighborhoods (Δ = 3.4 °C), indicating an associational thermal gradient along socioeconomic lines. These findings suggest that urban greening strategies should be calibrated to local population-density transition bands, and that surface heat mitigation planning should explicitly account for the unequal spatial distribution of surface thermal exposure across socioeconomic groups.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107872.title: Quantifying the effects of lift-up building morphology on pedestrian-level wind and comfort in dense urban arrays: A data-driven study
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107872.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107872.abstract: Pedestrian-level wind (PLW) strongly influences outdoor comfort in high-density cities. Lift-up buildings are widely adopted to enhance near-ground ventilation, yet the nonlinear aerodynamic interactions between their morphology and surrounding urban arrays remain insufficiently quantified. This study develops an integrated framework combining parametric CFD, surrogate modeling, and explainable machine learning to examine how lift-up building morphology influences pedestrian wind environments in dense urban arrays. A dataset of 180 cases was generated for a central lift-up building surrounded by low-rise buildings. The simulations were validated against wind-tunnel measurements, and a Random Forest surrogate model (R² = 0.966) enabled efficient prediction of pedestrian-level wind velocity and pressure-related indicators. Statistical analysis first identifies a morphological control hierarchy in which main-body height shows the strongest association with improved pedestrian-level ventilation, while plan proportions show weaker associations with airflow organization. To further reveal nonlinear relationships, SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) and one-dimensional accumulated local effects (ALE) were employed. Three key aerodynamic patterns emerge. First, increasing main-body height markedly improves ventilation, but the gains diminish at the upper sampled levels. Second, main-body aspect ratio and plan ratio exhibited non-monotonic responses, with lower unfavorable wind comfort ratios at intermediate values of approximately 1.5–2.0. Third, building height and wind orientation showed a pronounced interaction. Low-rise configurations showed greater contrasts between sampled alignments, whereas taller cases exhibited more favorable and less direction-sensitive pedestrian-level wind conditions. These findings clarify the nonlinear aerodynamic role of lift-up morphology and provide preliminary quantitative guidance for early-stage climate-responsive urban massing design within comparable dense-array settings.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107871.title: Decoding the spatiotemporal cascade effects of compound heat-flood risks in a sinking coastal city: A GCN-LSTM based multi-scenario projection
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107871.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107871.abstract: Global warming continues to exacerbate compound heat-flood risks in high-density coastal cities yet forecasting their nonlinear spatiotemporal cascade effects under land subsidence regulation remains highly challenging. This study aims to systematically identify the spatiotemporal evolution and underlying driving mechanisms of compound heat-flood risks in Jakarta across various subsidence gradients and future scenarios. We utilized the Hazard-Exposure-Vulnerability framework to quantify historical single and compound risks, specifically the Coupling Coordination Degree (CCD), from 2017 to 2024. Furthermore, a Graph Convolutional Network and Long Short-Term Memory (GCN-LSTM) model, integrated with GeoShapley spatial attribution, was developed to dynamically project risk evolution under Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs) from the year 2025 to 2050. The results indicate: (1) The compound heat-flood risk exhibits a significant non-linear synergetic pattern, with high-CCD zones remaining primarily concentrated in the northern coastal and central built-up areas, with growing compound risk pressure in the southern HSZ. (2) Impervious surface area acts as the primary anthropogenic driver escalating both hazards, while land subsidence substantially amplifies flood retention and compound stress in the southern region. (3) Multi-scenario projections reveal a structural breakpoint around 2035, after which the risk trajectories under different SSPs diverge more clearly. (4) Differentiated spatial interventions balance local geological constraints, enabling the highly vulnerable high subsidence zones (HSZ) to achieve the most significant risk mitigation. Ultimately, prioritizing localized groundwater control and spatial ecological renewal is absolutely crucial for cutting the destructive cascade transmission and achieving resilient urban development.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107880.title: Towards an urban digital twin: An XAI-integrated prototype framework for sustainable mobility modelling in Algiers, Algeria
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107880.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107880.abstract: Rapid urbanisation across North African metropolises—Algiers in particular—places transport systems under mounting stress: congestion erodes economic productivity, vehicle emissions degrade public health, and energy-intensive mobility patterns accelerate carbon expenditure. These pressures are compounded by the absence of interpretable tools capable of jointly quantifying congestion, energy demand, and air quality in forms actionable for governance. This underscores the need for integrated spatiotemporal modeling of traffic congestion, energy demand, and air quality for sustainable urban mobility planning. This study constructs, validates, and applies a prototype framework towards an Urban Digital Twin for Algiers, integrating eight heterogeneous urban data streams within a unified geospatial environment to jointly model traffic congestion, energy demand, and air quality. A comprehensive hybrid dataset, comprising directly observed and statistically augmented records for model robustness, encompasses 500,000 spatiotemporal records across 5,000 road segments and 57 communes. Random Forest and XGBoost models were benchmarked with SHAP attribution and scenario simulation. The proposed framework provides an exploratory, scenario-based decision-support tool directly applicable to the ongoing revision in Algiers. The Compact Mixed-Use and TOD scenarios demonstrate substantial energy and environmental gains—energy reduction and NO2 improvement—establishing a scenario-based, quantitative evidence base for transit-integrated land use revisions to Algiers' master planning frameworks, utilizing a hybrid dataset comprising both directly observed and statistically augmented records to directly inform temporally targeted demand management policy for North African cities.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107858.title: A continental-scale XGBoost framework for multi-hazard susceptibility and socioeconomic exposure in South America
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107858.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107858.abstract: Floods, droughts, and wildfires affect many South American cities, but continent-scale assessments rarely connect hazard susceptibility with urban exposure. We present a continental-scale (∼1 km) framework that compares a simple weighted benchmark with hazard-specific Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) models built from 27 Earth observation and socioeconomic datasets. On identical held-out test pixels, XGBoost increased ROC-AUC from 0.65 to 0.93 for flood, from 0.59 to 0.89 for drought, and from 0.74 to 0.92 for wildfire, with similar gains in PR-AUC, F1 score, and balanced accuracy. We therefore used XGBoost to generate the final susceptibility maps. The mapped classes are relative continental quantile classes, not absolute event probability thresholds. The mapped patterns place higher flood likelihood in humid lowlands and river corridors, higher drought likelihood in water-limited hot regions, and higher wildfire likelihood in hot, dry frontier regions. A city-scale synthesis for 758 South American cities places the strongest combinations of high composite hazard and lower adaptive capacity in northeastern Brazil, Caribbean-facing Colombia and Venezuela, and lowland Bolivia, while lower-hazard and stronger-capacity settings are more common in parts of the Southern Cone and Andean corridors. The maps, input layers, municipal classes, and city-level summaries can be explored in MIRA, the Multi-hazard Index for Risk Assessment, at https://riskframeworksa.github.io/data_viewer/.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107878.title: Fine-scale urban heat mapping by machine learning downscaling of MODIS land surface temperature in a hyper-arid megacity
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107878.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107878.abstract: Fine-scale land surface temperature (LST) underpins assessment of the surface urban heat island and heat exposure in cities, yet thermal sensors trade spatial detail against temporal frequency. Evaluate a reproducible machine learning framework that downscales seasonal-median MODIS daytime LST from 1 km to 100 m over the hyper-arid megacity of Greater Cairo, Egypt, for summer 2025. A scale-consistent regression of coarse LST on fine predictors—Sentinel-2 indices, terrain derivatives, and sub-pixel ESA WorldCover fractions—is combined with an additive residual correction; seven algorithms are compared. Products are assessed by cross-validation, scale-consistency on re-aggregation, and comparison with Landsat-8/9. At the coarse scale the predictor–LST relationship is strong (histogram gradient boosting: R² = 0.94, RMSE = 0.77 °C; 0.93–0.92 under 3–8 km blocking); re-aggregation shows approximate MODIS consistency (R² = 0.83–0.99, model-dependent; small bias for signal-consistent models); and the 100 m fields recover the intra-urban thermal pattern. Against Landsat, however, every product consistent with the coarse signal shows a large systematic cold bias (−5.5 to −6.1 °C) and a negative R², while retaining moderate spatial correlation (r up to 0.84); the bias is minimal over water and largest over built-up and bare surfaces. The un-downscaled MODIS field carries the same offset (−5.93 °C), as do twelve same-day pairs (−6.3 ± 2.0 °C), so it is inherited from the MODIS–Landsat product pair to within the empirically measured scale-consistency error, rather than being created by sharpening. Statistical sharpening faithfully redistributes the parent sensor’s information but cannot reconcile inter-sensor differences; a non-coincident finer image is not a valid absolute reference for downscaled urban LST.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107914.title: Research on spatial heterogeneity of urban flood susceptibility and model attribution in Beijing: An XGBoost-SHAP analysis based on spatial cross-validation
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107914.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107914.abstract: Urban waterlogging exhibits significant spatial autocorrelation and extreme class imbalance, which may lead to overestimation of model generalization performance when random data splits are used. Taking 68,104 500 m grid cells in Beijing as evaluation units, this study constructs an urban waterlogging susceptibility model based on 405 historically waterlogged positive samples and 16 static geo-socioeconomic indicators covering hazard, exposure, and vulnerability. Fivefold spatial block cross-validation at 0.1° resolution is employed to compare Logistic Regression, Random Forest, Linear SVM, LightGBM, CatBoost, and XGBoost, together with class-imbalance handling techniques including class weighting, SMOTE, Borderline-SMOTE, ADASYN, Balanced Random Forest, and EasyEnsemble. Results show that XGBoost achieves a spatial cross-validation ROC-AUC of 0.888±0.020 and a PR-AUC of 0.052±0.011, with a recall of 0.796±0.067 for the waterlogging class. Although it attains the highest PR-AUC among all models, its precision is only 0.024, indicating that the model is better suited as a high-recall screening tool than as a deterministic forecasting system. ROC-AUC values across the three pseudo-negative sampling strategies range from 0.882 to 0.887, and the SHAP rankings of slope, population density, and vegetation coverage remain generally stable. Full-sample SHAP attribution identifies slope, vegetation coverage, total population, and elevation as the most influential variables. Breakpoints derived from piecewise regression are interpreted as internal statistical associations within the model rather than as hydrological or planning thresholds. . Street typology based on 19 aggregated indicators retained eight principal components explaining 92.3% of variance. Although K=2 achieved the highest silhouette coefficient (0.375), the K=5 solution was retained for governance-oriented classification because its seed stability was high (mean ARI = 0.991) and its 80% subsample stability remained acceptable (ARI = 0.891 ± 0.090). Its silhouette coefficient was 0.221, so it is not presented as the unique statistical optimum. This study repositions the model from "risk prediction" to "static susceptibility identification," while explicitly acknowledging limitations arising from unobserved factors such as drainage network capacity, pumping station performance, event rainfall characteristics, and monitoring biases.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107913.title: Dual friction mapping of urban pedestrian spaces: Integrating street-view visual analytics and Geographically Neural Network Weighted Regression in Izmir, Türkiye
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107913.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107913.abstract: Pedestrian comfort is undermined both by physical obstructions that compress usable sidewalk space and by thermal stress in hot weather. Yet physical and thermal friction are usually measured separately, leaving planners without a fine-grained basis for deciding where obstacle removal, sidewalk widening, or shade and cooling interventions are actually needed. This study introduces the Pedestrian Friction Index (PFI), combining a Physical Comfort Score (visual obstruction from street-view imagery, including effective clear walking width) and a Thermal Friction Score (land surface temperature, albedo, greenery, and sky openness) in equal measure, applied across 5663 street-view points in Izmir, Türkiye. Street-view images were segmented for physical indicators, while satellite imagery supplied thermal and terrain metrics. We modelled PFI using Geographically Neural Network Weighted Regression (GNNWR), allowing spatial non-stationarity across the city, and benchmarked it against four spatial regression models. GNNWR achieved an out-of-sample R2 of 0.407 under repeated hex-blocked cross-validation. Local coefficients indicated that clear walking width and tree canopy height consistently reduced friction, whereas morphological density, street canyon ratio, ground coverage, and park distance increased it in specific spatial contexts. A bivariate vulnerability atlas identified locations where high physical and thermal friction coincide, guiding sidewalk widening, obstacle removal, tree planting, and heat mitigation in Mediterranean cities. The findings support a planning transition from generic walkability rankings to diagnosis-specific pedestrian infrastructure policy.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107884.title: Urban wind field reconstruction for low-altitude flight: A comparison of Gappy POD and deep autoencoder strategies using CFD and sparse sensing
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107884.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107884.abstract: Urban wind field reconstruction from sparse observations is important for real-time monitoring, Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) flight safety, and smart city applications. However, accurately recovering complex wind fields in dense urban areas remains challenging because building-induced flow distortion creates strong spatial heterogeneity. In this study, four reconstruction frameworks, namely Gappy Proper Orthogonal Decomposition (POD), Gappy POD combined with fully-connected Neural Networks (POD+NN), Autoencoder (AE), and AE combined with NN (AE+NN), are developed and evaluated for sparse sensor urban wind field reconstruction using a high-resolution CFD database for a central district in Shenzhen. The results show that deep learning-based methods outperform the traditional linear Gappy POD approach, with AE+NN achieving the best overall accuracy and robustness. At 120 m height, which is highly relevant to low-altitude UAV applications, AE+NN reduces wind speed reconstruction errors by about 20–30% compared with Gappy POD. AE+NN also remains stable under sparse sensor configurations, whereas Gappy POD requires substantially more sensors to avoid large errors. Reconstruction accuracy is strongly influenced by height and wind direction, while the effect of sensor layout (randomly or uniformly distributed) is comparatively small. AE-based methods show stronger generalization across wind directions and better reproduce local wind variations and wake-affected regions along representative UAV trajectories. In addition, introducing a physics-based regularization term improves the spatial consistency of AE reconstruction by reducing physically inconsistent solutions and narrowing the full-field error distribution. This study demonstrates that combining nonlinear manifold learning with latent-variable prediction provides an efficient and accurate framework for sparse sensor urban wind reconstruction. The proposed AE+NN approach shows strong potential for practical applications such as UAV route planning, urban wind hazard assessment, and smart-city wind monitoring.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107968.title: Assessing vulnerability to compound heatwave-ozone events using explainable machine learning: Evidence from the Greater Bay Area, China
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107968.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107968.abstract: Compound Heatwave–Ozone Events (CHOE) are emerging as major environmental health challenges in rapidly urbanizing regions, yet how urban morphology is associated with their vulnerability patterns remains poorly understood. Because compound heatwave–ozone risk involves overlapping but non-identical environmental controls, the morphology-dependence of vulnerability cannot be inferred directly from single-hazard studies. This study characterizes the spatial organization of CHOE vulnerability across urban morphologies and identifies the factors most strongly associated with it, using the Guangdong–Hong Kong–Macao Greater Bay Area as a case. A CHOE vulnerability index (CHOE-VI) is constructed within an Exposure–Sensitivity–Adaptive Capacity framework, and Local Climate Zones (LCZs) are combined with an XGBoost–SHAP approach to decompose indicator contributions across dominant LCZ classes. The results show that CHOE-VI exhibits a pronounced core–periphery gradient, with the main hotspots concentrated in the dense built-up corridor of the Guangzhou–Foshan urban core. Exposure forms the dominant baseline of CHOE-VI, while sensitivity and adaptive-capacity conditions further differentiate its spatial pattern across urban morphologies. Surface hardening, atmospheric ventilation, human activity intensity, and coastal location are the highest-ranked conditions. SHAP results reveal an imbalance between risk-amplifying and adaptive-capacity-related contributions in LCZ 1 and LCZ 2, with the former exceeding the latter in magnitude for the selected indicators, whereas in vegetated LCZs, CHOE-VI is associated mainly with ventilation and coastal conditions. These findings inform morphology-sensitive, spatially differentiated adaptation strategies for densely urbanized coastal regions.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.108004.title: From optimization to generation: A machine learning and morphology-constrained GAN framework for improving energy and thermal performance in residential clusters
10.1016/j.scs.2026.108004.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.108004.abstract: Urban morphology substantially affects energy and thermal performance in residential clusters. However, existing studies have mainly focused on performance prediction or parametric optimization, with limited attention to translating optimized parameters into spatial layout solutions. This study proposes an optimization-generation framework that combines machine learning and a morphology-constrained generative adversarial network (MCGAN) for residential clusters. Using 5466 samples from five representative climate zones in China, four performance indicators were computed: energy use intensity (EUI), solar energy generation intensity (SEGI), net energy use intensity (NEUI), and outdoor thermal comfort autonomy (OTCA). Machine learning-based surrogate models and SHAP (Shapley Additive exPlanations) analysis were used to predict performance and identify dominant morphological drivers. The best-performing surrogate model was integrated with the non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm II (NSGA-II) and MCGAN to generate residential layouts from optimized morphological parameters. The results indicate that energy-related indicators are mainly influenced by the perimeter-to-area ratio and facade-to-roof area ratio, whereas outdoor thermal comfort is primarily governed by the sky view factor and buildings enclosure ratio. XGBoost and LightGBM achieved the highest predictive accuracy, with R² values exceeding 0.89 across all indicators. A residential cluster in Wuhan was used to validate the proposed framework, where 1211 candidate layouts were generated and 161 Pareto-optimal solutions were identified through the optimization-to-generation process. Equal-weight TOPSIS evaluation of the re-simulation results indicated that the optimized schemes achieved better overall performance than the original design. The proposed framework provides interpretable decision support for early-stage residential cluster planning and design.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107986.title: Spatiotemporal evolution and spatially heterogeneous drivers of urban flood risk: A K-means optimized XGBoost model
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107986.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107986.abstract: With the intensification of climate change and rapid urbanization, urban flooding events have become increasingly frequent, posing serious threats to urban safety and sustainable development. However, existing studies often regard cities as homogeneous spaces, which limits the understanding of spatially heterogeneous flood drivers. Taking the Ningbo urban area as the study area, historical urban flood points from 2010 to 2024 collected from social media and government websites were analyzed using kernel density estimation and standard deviational ellipse analysis to reveal spatiotemporal evolution patterns. Based on flood records and multisource influencing factors, a K-means optimized XGBoost (KXGBoost) model was developed, combined with SHAP and Partial Dependence Plot (PDP) analyses to interpret the contributions and nonlinear response patterns of key factors across different zones. The results show that high and very high risk areas were mainly distributed in the central urban area, and the spatial pattern of urban flooding evolved from a highly concentrated monocentric pattern toward a more dispersed and polycentric pattern. The KXGBoost model considering spatial heterogeneity improved the AUC from 0.84 to 0.89 compared with the baseline XGBoost model. The highly urbanized Zone 1 was mainly influenced by Drainage, Road and NDVI, whereas Zone 3 showed higher contributions from NDVI, Road and MBH. PDP results further revealed nonlinear relationships of drainage density and vegetation coverage with flood risk, and these response patterns varied under different road and building conditions. These findings provide scientific support for differentiated urban flood management strategies and enhance urban resilience under climate change.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.108012.title: Investigating the Nonlinear and Spatially Heterogeneous Impacts of Urban Form on Land Surface Temperature Using Geographic Explainable Artificial Intelligence
10.1016/j.scs.2026.108012.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.108012.abstract:
ABSTRACT
Previous studies have extensively examined urban form–land surface temperature (LST) relationships. However, nonlinear responses, spatiotemporal heterogeneity, and local predictive contributions have not been adequately examined within a unified framework. This study examines these relationships in Sana’a City, Yemen, using multi-temporal Landsat data from 2005, 2015, and 2025 within a geographically and temporally weighted random forest–GeoShapley (GTWRF–GeoShapley) framework. The analysis distinguishes local linear sensitivity, unsigned local random-forest importance, and signed predictive attribution. Results indicate that elevated LST has progressively expanded from the urban core into developing peripheral zones, with the area exceeding 25°C increasing from 22% to 47%. Spatially, regions of grid cells dominated by built-environment indicators increased from 28% to 50%, while the proportion dominated by vegetation-related indicators declined from 72% to 50%. Positive contributions associated with the Normalized Difference Built-up Index (NDBI) and built-up density (BUD) became increasingly spatially contiguous across central built-up areas; the mean absolute GeoShapley contribution of NDBI increased from 0.52 to 0.60°C, while BUD remained stable at approximately 0.50°C. Urban compactness exhibited a localized core–periphery pattern, with the largest proportional increase in mean absolute contribution (+25.0%). Conversely, cooling contributions associated with vegetation fraction became increasingly fragmented and were largely confined to less urbanized peripheral areas. Furthermore, BUD exhibited a nonlinear warming response, with its positive contribution increasing from +1.2 to +1.6°C beyond an empirical transition near 30% BUD. These findings provide geographically explicit insights for managing urban growth. Strategies aimed at preventing fragmented built-up expansion from reducing connected green spaces and generating localized thermal hotspots could help curb fragmented urban expansion at city fringes, ultimately supporting sustainable morphological transitions for rapidly growing cities.
keywords: Geographically and temporally weighted random forest

10.1016/j.scs.2026.108038.title: A geospatial decision support system for infrastructure planning: a GIS-machine learning-MCDM framework with an application to EV charging station planning
10.1016/j.scs.2026.108038.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.108038.abstract: Transportation is a major producer of greenhouse gases (GHGs), making its decarbonization a worldwide challenge. EVs are an effective way to reduce transportation-related GHG emissions. However, the limited and uneven distribution of Electric Vehicle Charging Stations (EVCSs) remains a major barrier to EV adoption, particularly in Italy. Recent EVCS planning studies increasingly integrate Geographic Information Systems (GIS), multi-criteria decision-making (MCDM), and machine learning (ML) for spatial suitability assessment. However, limited attention has been given to comparing expert-based and data-driven suitability, assessing their spatial robustness, and translating these patterns into prioritized areas for EVCS planning. This study develops a transferable Geospatial Decision Support System (GeoSDSS) that integrates GIS, AHP, Random Forest (RF), and TOPSIS to support reliable, evidence-based EVCS site selection. GIS-based processing is applied to socio-economic, transport, environmental, and infrastructure datasets. Criterion weights are derived from both AHP and two RF models including Random Forest Regression-Based Suitability Scoring (RFSS) and Random Forest Presence-Absence Classification (RF-PA), a combination of expert judgment and data-driven learning. The framework systematically compares expert-based and data-driven approaches by evaluating their spatial patterns and independent predictive performance to identify robust suitability areas for infrastructure planning. RF model reliability is evaluated using conventional cross-validation and leave-one-province-out spatial cross-validation. RF-PA maintained strong classification performance under geographically independent validation, achieving a mean ROC-AUC of 0.974 across the five provinces. Furthermore, independent external validation using previously unseen locations demonstrate that RF-PA achieved the strongest predictive performance among the evaluated approaches, with an AUC of 0.9408, Kappa of 0.6782, TSS of 0.6782, and accuracy of 83.91%. TOPSIS is subsequently applied to the RF-PA suitability assessment to transform predicted suitability into a spatial prioritization surface, identifying 356.64 km² (2.09%) as high-to-very-high priority areas for EVCS planning. The comparison of suitability maps indicates strong spatial consistency between RF-PA and AHP, with approximately 224.20 km² of overlapping highly suitable areas, under the selected thresholds. Tourism and accessibility factors, including tourism zones, attraction areas, and parking facilities, are identified as the most influential variables. Rome shows the highest concentration of suitable locations, while Rieti shows the lowest and most fragmented distribution. The results suggest that existing EVCS deployment patterns in Lazio are more strongly associated with destination-based mobility factors than residential density. The proposed GeoSDSS provides a transferable framework for integrating empirical infrastructure patterns, expert knowledge, model validation, and spatial prioritization to support evidence-based EVCS planning and provides a transferable decision-support tool for urban and regional infrastructure planning, with potential applications in smart cities and sustainable mobility.

10.1016/j.scs.2026.107981.title: Deep reinforcement learning-based UAV navigation in 3D urban boundary layers
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107981.source: ScienceDirect official citation and abstract BibTeX export
10.1016/j.scs.2026.107981.abstract: Low-altitude unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) navigation in urban environments is challenged by complex building geometry and unsteady wind disturbances, including wakes, recirculation, and vertical motions within the urban boundary layer (UBL). To improve autonomous navigation under partial observation and unsteady wind disturbances, this study proposes a Latent actor and Random Network Distillation (RND) augmented Soft actor critic method (LARA-SAC). A high-fidelity three-dimensional (3D) unsteady urban wind field generated by large-eddy simulation (LES) is incorporated into the navigation environment, enabling the agent to learn continuous control policies under explicit building constraints and wind forcing. LARA-SAC integrates historical observation memory, latent trajectory exploration, and state action novelty estimation within the SAC framework. A history queue and a Gated Transformer eXtra Large (GTrXL) encoder extract recent wind disturbances, target direction changes, and obstacle approach trends, while latent exploration improves directional consistency and RND enhances early value learning through novelty feedback. Compared with recent benchmark methods, LARA-SAC shows more stable learning behavior, stronger task completion ability, and lower collision risk.
